The court shall grant the motion only if it determines that the opinion establishes a new rule of law, applies an existing rule to a significantly different factual situation, or conflicts with another published decision.

A decision of the Court of Appeals becomes final and operative upon the expiration of the time for filing a petition for leave to appeal, or upon the denial of such a petition by the Supreme Court. If a timely petition is filed, the decision remains stayed until the Supreme Court disposes of the petition or remands the case.

Upon voting to seat a conflict panel, the Court of Appeals shall immediately notify the Supreme Court in writing. The notification must specify the identity of the assigned judges and the case caption. This report is mandatory regardless of whether the vote was unanimous or divided. No further action by the parties is required to trigger this reporting obligation.

On motion of any party, the Court of Appeals may award damages for frivolous appeal if it finds the appeal was filed solely to delay proceedings or harass. The court shall assess costs against the appellant and counsel. A party seeking such relief must file a motion within ten days after entry of judgment. The court may impose sanctions upon finding bad faith or lack of merit.

If no transcript is ordered within thirty days after filing notice of appeal, the clerk shall notify the appellant. If the appellant fails to order the transcript or file a brief within sixty days of that notice, the court may dismiss the appeal on motion of any party or sua sponte. The presiding judge shall enter the order of dismissal.

A party seeking costs must file an itemized bill with the clerk within fourteen days after entry of the final disposition. If a motion for reconsideration is filed, the time to file the bill runs from the date of the order denying the motion. Failure to file within this period constitutes a waiver of the right to recover costs.

Upon receipt of the Commission’s recommendation for removal, the Supreme Court shall convene to consider the matter. The Court must determine whether probable cause exists to believe the judge has committed misconduct warranting removal. If probable cause is found, the Court shall appoint a special master or proceed directly to trial. No further motion or leave of court is required to initiate this review.

A party may petition the Supreme Court for leave to appeal from a published opinion of the Court of Appeals if that opinion conflicts with another published opinion of the Court of Appeals on the same question of law. The petition must be filed within twenty-one days after entry of the Court of Appeals’ order disposing of the case.

If the Court of Appeals remands a case for further proceedings, the time to file a notice of appeal to the Supreme Court runs from the entry of the order denying a motion for reconsideration or other post-remand relief, if such motion is filed within the time prescribed by rule. Otherwise, the time runs from the entry of the remand order.

A party may appeal from an order entered after remand. The appeal is limited to issues arising from the post-remand proceedings, unless the Court of Appeals expressly reserved jurisdiction over prior claims. A petition for leave to appeal must be filed within twenty-one days after entry of the order.

A party may file a reply brief within seven days after service of the answer. The reply must be served on all parties. No more than ten copies shall be filed with the clerk, unless the court orders otherwise. A reply addressing matters not raised in the answer requires leave of court. Failure to comply with these requirements constitutes grounds for striking the reply.

A nonparty seeking to file an amicus curiae brief in support of an application for leave to appeal must first obtain written consent from all parties or permission of the Court on motion. If permission is granted, the amicus brief shall be filed within ten days after entry of the order granting permission, unless the Court specifies a different time period.

Upon denial of leave to appeal, the judgment or order of the Court of Appeals becomes final. A party may enforce the judgment immediately upon receipt of notice of the Supreme Court’s denial. No stay is in effect unless expressly ordered by the Supreme Court or the Court of Appeals prior to the denial.

In an original action challenging presidential election certification, the Court shall issue its final order no later than six days before the electors meet to cast their votes. An order issued after this deadline is not binding on state officials or federal authorities for purposes of determining certified results. The Court may extend this period only upon a showing of extraordinary circumstances that do not delay the electoral process.

A party seeking to cross-appeal must file a notice within fourteen days after the opposing party files an application for leave to appeal. Failure to file within this period constitutes a waiver of the right to cross-appeal. The court may not extend this time limit, nor shall it grant relief from the deadline for any reason, including excusable neglect or inadvertence.

On motion by the Governor, the Supreme Court may certify a controlling public-law question from a pending trial court action. Upon certification, the trial court shall stay proceedings until the Supreme Court resolves the certified question. The lower court must transmit the record within ten days of the order. Parties shall file briefs on the merits within thirty days thereafter.

A party may file a motion for rehearing within 21 days after entry of the order denying leave to appeal. The motion shall state with particularity the points of law or fact believed to have been overlooked or misapprehended. If the motion is denied, no further application for review may be filed in this Court regarding the same matter.

A party who is both an appellee and a cross-appellant may file a single brief addressing both appeals. The brief must be filed within forty-two days after entry of the order granting leave to appeal or filing the notice of appeal, whichever occurs later. The brief shall contain separate sections for the response and the cross-appeal, clearly designated as such.

On motion or sua sponte, the court may impose sanctions for frivolous conduct, including misrepresentation of the record in briefs. Sanctions shall be imposed only after notice and an opportunity to respond. The court may order payment of reasonable attorney fees and costs incurred as a result of such improper conduct.

If no record is filed within sixty days after notice of appeal, the clerk shall dismiss the appeal. A party may move to reinstate the appeal within thirty days after dismissal. The court shall grant the motion if good cause is shown for the failure to file the record. Failure to move within thirty days results in final dismissal.

On motion of all parties, the Court may dismiss an appeal pending before it. The motion must state that the case has been settled or otherwise resolved. If filed within seven days of oral argument, the moving party shall pay any costs incurred by the opposing party in preparing for argument. The Clerk shall enter judgment dismissing the appeal upon approval.

A party unable to pay fees may file an application for leave to proceed without prepayment. The application shall be filed with the required documents. No fee is charged for the application. If the court denies the application, the party must pay the original filing fee within ten days of denial or the action shall be dismissed for failure to prosecute.

The administrative rules in this chapter apply to all trial courts, including circuit, district, and probate courts. Each court shall adopt local rules consistent with these provisions within ninety days of adoption. The Chief Justice may issue orders necessary to implement uniform administration across all judicial districts. Compliance is mandatory for all judicial officers and court personnel.

A party may record proceedings using personal equipment only with prior court approval. Upon request, the court shall permit such recording if it does not disrupt the hearing. All recordings remain the property of the party and may be used for case preparation. The court may impose conditions to protect confidentiality or prevent prejudice. Unauthorized dissemination is prohibited unless ordered by the court.

The chief judge shall be selected by majority vote of the active judges of the court. No formal application is required. Selection must occur within thirty days after a vacancy arises or upon expiration of the term. If no selection is made within that period, the senior active judge shall serve as chief judge until a successor is chosen.

The chief judge of each circuit court shall establish the hours of operation and determine the minimum number of judges and staff required to be present during those hours. These determinations must ensure adequate access to justice and efficient administration of judicial business. The chief judge may modify these requirements upon finding that existing arrangements are insufficient or inefficient, subject to approval by the Administrative Office of the Courts.

The chief judge shall report to the state court administrator each quarter any felony case pending disposition for more than one year after bindover. The report must include the case number, defendant name, and date of bindover. This reporting requirement applies only to cases where no final judgment has been entered within twelve months of the binding over order.

The chief judge must report to the state court administrator all misdemeanor and ordinance cases pending for more than one hundred eighty days. This period is computed from the date of arrest or issuance of a summons. Cases pending less than one hundred eighty days need not be listed on the quarterly criminal caseload report, provided they are actively being processed by the court.

A judge attending judicial education programs outside the state judicial conference must obtain prior approval from the Chief Justice or designee. Such attendance shall count against the annual twenty-day allotment for professional development. Requests for approval must be submitted in writing at least thirty days before the program begins, detailing the curriculum and relevance to judicial duties.

Upon recusal or disqualification, the chief judge shall reassign the case without stating cause. The successor judge is selected by lot or rotation. Within three days of assignment, the clerk must serve written notice on all parties identifying the new judge and setting a preliminary conference date. No motion to vacate the reassignment order is permitted unless fraud or conflict of interest is alleged.

A court shall solicit comments from the local bar association before adopting a local rule. The court must transmit the proposed rule, together with any comments received, to the Administrative Office of the Courts within thirty days after adoption. The rule becomes effective only upon approval by the Supreme Court or the Chief Justice, as applicable.

During trial, spectators in the gallery shall not communicate with any witness while that witness is testifying. Such communication includes electronic messaging, texting, or other digital transmission. The court may impose additional restrictions on electronic device usage to preserve decorum and prevent interference with judicial proceedings. Violations constitute contempt of court.

On motion to close the courtroom, the court must find that closure is no broader than necessary to protect the identified interest. The order shall specify the duration of closure and limit it strictly to the testimony requiring exclusion. General closures are prohibited. The court must make specific findings on the record demonstrating that less restrictive alternatives were considered and rejected before ordering any closure.

Any person adversely affected by an order closing proceedings may file a motion to reopen within seven days of entry. If the court denies the motion, the movant may seek immediate appellate review pursuant to MCR 7.213(A). The application for leave must be filed with the trial court within fourteen days of denial and served on all parties.

The plaintiff must designate one primary case type upon filing the initial pleading. Where multiple causes of action exist, the court may assign additional codes. This designation governs all subsequent filings unless amended by order. The clerk shall maintain the primary code for docketing purposes. Parties may request reclassification on motion showing good cause.

A clerk shall accept for filing any document that is properly prepared and filed in accordance with these rules. A clerk may reject a filing only if the document fails to comply with formatting requirements, lacks required fees, or is otherwise legally insufficient on its face. The clerk must provide written notice of rejection stating specific grounds.

When an item is filed electronically and enters the chronological record without manual entry by a deputy clerk, the system shall automatically assign the initials of the filing party or attorney to that entry. This automated designation serves as the official record of receipt and supersedes any requirement for clerical initialing in such instances.

Upon migration of legacy scanned filings to the statewide case management system, the clerk shall maintain a thirty-day hold on public access. After thirty days, unless sealed by court order or exempted by statute, the filings shall be immediately available for public inspection and copying through the electronic filing system.

A clerk shall charge fees for copies of records at rates established by the State Court Administrative Office. Fees shall not include capital costs, depreciation, or amortization of imaging systems or equipment. Charges must reflect only direct reproduction expenses. Any fee schedule incorporating indirect overhead costs is prohibited and subject to immediate correction upon motion by any party.

An attorney’s fee award against an insurer under statute shall not be applied toward the statutory percentage limitation on contingency fees. Fees derived from such statutory awards are excluded from the calculation of total compensation for purposes of determining compliance with maximum allowable percentages. The court shall treat statutory fee recoveries as separate from client-funded contingency arrangements when assessing fee reasonableness and statutory caps.

The affidavit of the sponsoring attorney must state that the out-of-state lawyer has not appeared in more than five Michigan cases within the preceding twenty-four months, or explain why such limitation does not apply. The affidavit shall also certify that the applicant is authorized to practice law in another jurisdiction and is of good standing.

A party’s participation in an administrative complaint regarding interpreter competence shall not constitute a waiver of the right to raise such issues in the underlying proceeding or on appeal. Preservation of error requires timely objection at trial. Failure to object constitutes waiver, regardless of any parallel administrative proceedings. The court may consider administrative findings as evidence of incompetence.

The clerk of the court shall maintain current contact information for all magistrates assigned to the district. Upon request by a party or upon the magistrate’s removal from service, the clerk shall promptly provide such details to the requesting party or successor magistrate, ensuring continuity of proceedings and proper notification of judicial assignments within the district.

Upon final disposition of the proceeding, the clerk shall retain the original will in the court file for five years. After such period, unless the will is under seal or otherwise ordered retained by the court, the clerk may destroy the document in accordance with state records retention schedules. The clerk shall provide notice to interested parties before destruction if required by statute.

The current disciplinary rules govern all pending proceedings and apply to conduct occurring prior to their effective date. These rules shall be construed to effectuate their general purpose to make uniform the practice and procedure under the rules, promote simplicity in administration, and secure just determination. No right, privilege, or duty heretofore acquired shall be impaired by this adoption.

A respondent must file an answer to a grievance within twenty-one days after service of the complaint. The answer shall specifically deny each allegation or admit it in part. General denials are insufficient. Arguments based on industry custom, prevalence of conduct among other attorneys, or absence of prior disciplinary action are not valid defenses and shall be disregarded by the court in determining liability.

The Chief Justice shall appoint the chair of the Attorney Grievance Commission for a term of two years. No person may serve more than two consecutive terms as chair. The appointment must be made within thirty days following the expiration of the preceding chair’s term or upon vacancy. Reappointment is prohibited if the individual has completed two full consecutive terms.

The Chief Judge of the Attorney Grievance Commission shall appoint and remove the Executive Director. Removal shall occur only for cause, including incompetence, misconduct, or neglect of duty. No removal may be effected without prior written notice and a reasonable opportunity to respond. The Chief Judge must file a certificate of appointment or removal with the Clerk of the Supreme Court within ten days of the action.

Upon learning of a pending confidential grievance involving himself, a panelist shall immediately disclose this fact to the parties and withdraw from service. The disclosure must occur within three days of such knowledge. Failure to disclose constitutes grounds for disqualification upon motion by any party. The presiding officer may extend this time for good cause shown.

Upon determining that a grievance lacks merit or is frivolous, the administrator may dismiss it without referral to the commission. The administrator shall notify the respondent lawyer in writing of the dismissal within ten days. The notice must state the reasons for dismissal and advise the lawyer of the right to request reinstatement of the grievance by filing a written motion with the commission within twenty days of receipt.

Within fourteen days after service of the order accepting the admonition, a respondent may file a motion to withdraw acceptance or object to the sanction. If no such motion is filed within the prescribed time, the grievance commission shall certify the matter as closed and transmit the final record to the Board of Commissioners of Grievances for entry on the public register.

The Administrator shall produce all exhibits to the respondent within ten days after service of the notice of hearing. Any exhibit not produced within this period is inadmissible, unless the panel finds good cause for late production. Exhibits supplied during the week immediately preceding the hearing are presumptively excluded from evidence.

The respondent may offer to surrender the license to practice law in exchange for an agreed sanction. Such agreement is ineffective unless accepted by the Attorney Grievance Commission and approved by the Supreme Court. No stipulation regarding discipline shall bind the parties or the court without such acceptance and approval.

The written stipulation must specify the proposed discipline based on respondent’s admissions and prior history. It need not cite external benchmarks. The grievance administrator shall review the stipulation for consistency with disciplinary standards. If consistent, the administrator may approve the sanction without further proceedings. Approval requires that the proposed discipline adequately addresses the misconduct and serves the interests of justice and public protection.

Upon denial of a negotiated discipline proposal, the panel shall issue a written order specifying the reasons for rejection. A party may file an amended proposal addressing those deficiencies within fourteen days of service. The panel shall consider the amended proposal without further hearing unless good cause is shown. Failure to file within the prescribed time constitutes waiver of the right to submit revised terms.

Upon dismissal of charges against a referee by the Tenure Commission, the Commission shall immediately notify the referee and the Chief Justice. The notice must state that the charges are dismissed and specify the effective date. No further action is required unless the Commission determines additional proceedings are necessary under applicable law or rule.

Within twenty-one days after filing of the report, a party may file objections to findings or recommendations. Failure to object constitutes waiver. The court shall review de novo any objectioned findings. Unobjected findings are adopted unless clearly erroneous. The court retains authority to accept, reject, or modify recommendations.

Upon receipt of final discipline from another jurisdiction, the Board shall issue notice to the respondent. The out-of-state misconduct finding is conclusive unless the respondent proves by clear and convincing evidence that the other proceeding lacked due process or resulted in fundamentally unfair results. The respondent must file a motion contesting reciprocal discipline within twenty-one days of service.

On motion, the court may appoint an independent examiner. The report shall be disclosed to all parties prior to trial. If any party objects to the examiner’s testimony, the court may exclude the report unless the examiner is called as a witness. The party seeking admission of the report shall bear the cost of securing the examiner’s attendance and compensation for testimony.

On motion by the State Bar or sua sponte, the court may order an attorney respondent to submit to a psychological or medical evaluation regarding fitness to practice. If the respondent refuses to comply with such an order within fourteen days, the court shall deem the allegations of unfitness admitted and may impose sanctions, including immediate suspension from the practice of law, pending further proceedings.

The panel may impose additional conditions of probation beyond those specified in this rule when necessary to protect the public or ensure compliance. Such conditions shall be reasonable, related to the misconduct, and clearly stated in the order. The respondent must comply with all imposed conditions during the probationary period. Failure to comply constitutes grounds for immediate suspension.

Probation shall not exceed five years. The court may extend probation upon finding good cause. An attorney may move for early termination after serving two years. The court shall grant the motion if the attorney demonstrates sustained compliance and rehabilitation. Extensions require notice to the Board of Commissioners of Character and Fitness.

An attorney inactive due to disability may petition for reinstatement every twelve months. The petitioner must prove current competence and fitness to practice law. If inactive for more than five years, the petitioner shall also demonstrate completion of continuing legal education requirements prescribed by the Board of Commissioners of State Bar Rules.

An attorney suspended for twelve months must file an affidavit of compliance with the Administrator not earlier than thirty days before the suspension expires. Upon receipt of a complete affidavit, the Administrator shall restore the attorney’s license automatically unless the Administrator finds probable cause that the attorney has failed to comply with the suspension order or other disciplinary requirements.

The petitioner shall file a sworn statement detailing all financial accounts held or co-signed during the preceding five years. This statement must specify account ownership, balances, and transaction history. Failure to disclose such information constitutes grounds for denial of reinstatement. The court may require additional documentation upon motion by any party within ten days of filing.

The petitioner shall pay the grievance administrator’s reasonable fees and expenses upon reinstatement. These costs cover investigation, hearing preparation, and administrative processing distinct from board expenses. Payment must be made within thirty days of the order granting reinstatement. Failure to pay constitutes grounds for vacating the reinstatement order. The court may enforce payment through contempt proceedings.

The panel shall schedule a hearing within thirty days of receiving the administrator’s findings. A party may move for a determination based solely on affidavits and records. Unless the panel orders otherwise, personal appearance is not required. The panel may require oral argument or in-person testimony if necessary to resolve material factual disputes regarding eligibility for reinstatement.

Upon closure of a grievance without formal charges, the respondent attorney may request disclosure of the outcome. The Board shall grant such request unless public release would violate applicable confidentiality laws or compromise ongoing investigations. Disclosure must occur within thirty days of the final order. The court retains discretion to seal records if necessary to protect judicial integrity.

Upon mailing notice of nonpayment, the attorney’s license is suspended immediately. No hearing is required for suspension. The attorney may petition the court to reinstate the license by proposing a payment plan. If the court approves the plan and the attorney complies, the suspension is stayed pending full satisfaction of the assessed amount.

The parties must execute a written agreement submitting the fee dispute to arbitration before filing. Upon completion of arbitration, the arbitrator shall file the award with the clerk of the court having jurisdiction over the grievance. The award is final and binding unless vacated by the court within thirty days of filing for fraud, corruption, or misconduct.

Upon final disposition of a complaint resulting in removal, suspension, or censure, the Commission may assess against the respondent judge all reasonable expenses incurred in investigating and prosecuting the complaint. The assessment shall be made within thirty days after entry of the final order. Payment must be made within sixty days unless otherwise ordered by the Commission.

A member of the Commission on Judicial Tenure who is the subject of an investigation shall recuse herself from all proceedings concerning that investigation. She must abstain from voting, deliberating, or participating in any decision regarding her own tenure. Failure to recuse renders any action taken by the Commission in that matter void.

Upon receipt of a complaint against a judicial candidate within sixty days of an election, the Commission shall not conduct a public hearing or issue a final determination until after the election concludes. The Commission may, however, take immediate interim action to protect the integrity of the judiciary if necessary. All other investigative proceedings shall remain confidential and suspended pending the resolution of the election.

If the executive director prosecutes the charges, the director shall appoint an independent special counsel to advise the commission. The special counsel shall possess full authority to investigate, prepare documents, and present evidence. This appointment must occur within ten days of the director’s decision to prosecute. The special counsel reports directly to the commission, ensuring impartiality in proceedings where the executive director serves as prosecutor.

The respondent judge shall file a written answer within twenty-one days after service of the complaint. The answer must respond to each allegation specifically. Failure to deny an allegation constitutes an admission thereof. The court may grant leave to amend or supplement the answer on motion for good cause shown. Pleading standards applicable in civil actions do not govern judicial misconduct proceedings.

The neutral arbitrator shall notify the parties of the hearing date at least fourteen days in advance. The arbitrator shall rule on any dispositive motion within ten days after submission of briefs or oral argument, whichever is later. Failure to comply with these time limits does not invalidate the proceedings unless a party demonstrates substantial prejudice.

Upon receipt of the hearing officer’s report, the Commission shall notify each party of the right to file written exceptions within fourteen days. No oral argument is permitted unless the Commission, on its own motion or upon a party’s request demonstrating good cause, orders otherwise. Failure to file timely exceptions constitutes a waiver of the right to challenge the findings.

Upon signing a negotiated resolution, the Commission shall submit its recommendation to the Court. The recommendation must address any prior disciplinary history relevant to the current matter. Unless otherwise ordered by the Court for good cause shown, the recommendation and all supporting materials regarding the judge’s prior discipline shall be filed as public records within ten days of execution.

Upon appeal to the Supreme Court, the Commission shall designate counsel to represent it. The attorney who prosecuted the complaint before the Commission shall not serve as counsel on the appeal unless expressly authorized by the Commission. All briefs and filings must comply with Supreme Court rules regarding judicial tenure proceedings.

In tenure proceedings, service of a formal complaint upon a sitting judge shall be made by certified mail, return receipt requested, addressed to the judge’s chambers. Personal service is prohibited. Proof of service must be filed with the Court Administrator within ten days after mailing. Failure to comply with this method of service renders the filing null and void.

The Commission shall adopt written policies governing the retention, storage, and disposition of records related to judicial complaints. These policies must specify the duration for which each record type is maintained and the procedures for its secure destruction or transfer upon expiration. The Commission shall implement these policies within ninety days of adoption and shall make them publicly available upon request.

A person who files a complaint with the judicial tenure body, or an attorney assisting in its preparation, is immune from civil liability for acts performed in good faith within the scope of their duties. This immunity applies regardless of the complaint’s merit. No court shall entertain a civil action against such persons arising from these activities.

The Commission shall develop and administer continuing legal education programs for judges regarding judicial ethics and conduct. The Commission may publish guidelines, advisory opinions, and other materials to assist judges in complying with the Code of Judicial Conduct. These educational activities shall be conducted at times and places designated by the Commission, subject to available resources and approval by the Supreme Court.

Upon the death or sudden incapacity of a solo practitioner, any member of the practitioner’s firm may substitute as counsel. The substituting attorney must file a notice of substitution within fourteen days. The court may require proof of authority. All pending proceedings shall continue without interruption unless the court orders otherwise on motion for good cause shown.

Upon a partner’s inability to practice, remaining attorneys may continue representation without court appointment if clients consent in writing. Such consent must be filed with the clerk within thirty days of the disability. Absent written consent, the court shall appoint counsel upon motion. Failure to file consent or secure appointment mandates withdrawal from all pending matters.

A lawyer winding down the practice of a suspended attorney who is adverse to a former client in an unrelated matter shall notify that client within fourteen days of becoming aware of the conflict. The notice must advise the client of the right to retain new counsel and request the return of files, unless disclosure is prohibited by other rules or law.

Fees awarded to an interim administrator constitute a lien on the suspended lawyer’s trust accounts and firm assets. The lien attaches as of the date of the court order appointing the administrator. The administrator shall file proof of claim within thirty days of the fee award. The court may enforce the lien against any property held by the firm or in the control of the administrator to satisfy the judgment.

An attorney appointed to wind down an inactive lawyer’s practice shall maintain professional liability insurance covering services rendered during the appointment. Coverage must remain in effect until the court discharges the appointee. Failure to maintain such insurance constitutes grounds for immediate removal and may result in disciplinary sanctions. The appointee shall file proof of coverage with the clerk within thirty days of appointment.

Upon assuming responsibility for winding down an attorney’s practice, a successor attorney may handle open matters only after providing the client with written notice specifying the identity of the successor, the scope of representation, and any change in fee arrangements. Such notice must be delivered within ten days of assumption of duties. The client shall have thirty days to object to the continuation of representation by the successor attorney.

These rules shall be known as the Michigan Court Rules. In citing a rule, the abbreviation MCR shall be used. A specific rule shall be cited by its number, for example, MCR 2.111. References to these rules in pleadings and other documents may use the abbreviation MCR.

If a conflict exists between a general rule and a rule specifically applicable to a particular court or proceeding, the specific rule governs. In the absence of a specific rule, the general rule applies. This provision ensures that specialized procedural requirements take precedence over broad directives when addressing unique judicial contexts or case types within the Michigan court system.

The court shall maintain electronic case records including metadata, system-generated entries, and audit trails created by the e-filing software. These data points constitute official case records for all purposes. Parties may inspect such records upon request. The clerk shall preserve these records in accordance with state archival standards.

If an order is entered orally on the record, the court shall promptly prepare and sign the written order. A party may submit a proposed order to the court within seven days after oral entry. The clerk shall file the signed order immediately upon receipt. Failure to file does not invalidate the order if it was correctly stated on the record.

A party seeking redaction of sensitive data from a trial exhibit shall file a motion specifying the items to be blacked out. No filing fee is required for such motions. The court may grant the request if it finds that public disclosure would cause substantial harm outweighing the public interest in access. The moving party must serve the motion on all other parties at least seven days before the hearing date.

On motion to seal exhibits, the court clerk shall immediately restrict public access to the designated materials pending judicial determination. The clerk must segregate such documents from the general file and maintain them under seal until the court enters an order granting or denying the motion. No party shall inspect sealed materials without prior leave of court.

Upon entry of an order restricting public access to specific exhibits, the clerk shall immediately seal those designated materials. All other filings within the same document that were not specifically identified in the court’s directive shall remain part of the public record and accessible to any person requesting inspection, unless otherwise ordered by the court or prohibited by law.

If the court orders that private contact information be redacted from the public file, the order shall designate an alternative address or telephone number for service of process and other communications. This substitute contact point must remain effective throughout the pendency of the action unless the court modifies the order upon a showing of good cause.

A clerk shall accept filings that omit social security numbers required by local forms. The court may not sanction a party or refuse acceptance solely because such information was left blank. Compliance with federal privacy mandates supersedes local form requirements. Parties must provide other identifying information as prescribed by rule.

A party may submit a settlement summary to the court for confidential review. Such submission shall not be filed with the clerk or entered into the public docket. The document must be marked “Confidential – For Judicial Review Only” and delivered directly to the assigned judge’s chambers. Unless otherwise ordered, the court shall maintain the summary outside the official case record to preserve settlement confidentiality.

A party may file a motion to excuse electronic filing for good cause. Good cause includes demonstrating that the party resides more than twenty-five miles from the nearest courthouse terminal, lacks reliable transportation to access such terminal, and possesses only limited technological resources at their residence insufficient for secure electronic submission. The court shall grant relief if the factual circumstances substantiate an undue hardship in complying with mandatory electronic filing requirements.

A party seeking exemption from electronic filing due to medical incapacity shall submit a written request to the clerk. No filing fee is required for processing such requests. The request need not be sworn unless the court specifically orders verification. The clerk shall grant the exemption upon receipt of the request, provided the stated condition prevents compliance with electronic filing requirements.

Upon a party’s withdrawal from electronic filing, paper documents filed with the court shall be deemed filed on the date of receipt by the clerk. If received after business hours, the document is filed on the next business day. This rule applies regardless of prior participation in the electronic filing system.

A party objecting to the court’s denial of an interpreter or allocation of costs must file a written objection within seven days after entry of the order. The objection shall state specific grounds for relief. Failure to file timely objection waives the right to appeal the ruling regarding language access services and associated financial responsibilities.

On motion to reconsider a denial of an interpreter, the clerk shall not collect any filing fee. The moving party must file the motion within fourteen days after entry of the order denying the request. The court may grant or deny the motion without oral argument unless otherwise ordered. This provision applies regardless of the normal filing charges applicable to other motions.

A party granted leave to proceed without cost in the trial court need not reapply for indigency status upon filing an interlocutory appeal, unless the appellate court orders otherwise. The waiver remains effective throughout the appellate proceedings. If the appellate court determines that circumstances have changed materially, it may require a new application within ten days of notice.

An incarcerated party seeking in forma pauperis status must attach to the application a sealed record from the Department of Corrections detailing current funds on hand and recent commissary activity. This attachment is mandatory regardless of other financial disclosures. Failure to include this specific documentation shall result in denial of the request without further hearing.

On motion for review of a denied fee waiver, the court may schedule a hearing. The applicant shall appear and present evidence establishing indigency. The court may grant or deny the application based on the record and oral argument. If granted, the order shall specify conditions, if any. Failure to appear constitutes abandonment of the motion.

A judge must disqualify themselves if they have a personal bias or prejudice concerning a party, or if they know that their impartiality might reasonably be questioned. This includes instances where the judge has a personal interest in the outcome of the proceeding that is more than de minimis. Disqualification shall occur upon the judge’s own motion or on timely motion by any party.

A party seeking recusal of a Supreme Court justice shall file a motion within ten days after learning of the disqualifying facts. If such facts arise less than ten days before the scheduled hearing, the motion may be filed immediately, provided it is served without delay. The court shall rule on the motion promptly to ensure timely adjudication.

On motion, if a judge denies recusal, a party may petition the full court for review within fourteen days. The full court shall rule on the petition without oral argument. No written order explaining the denial of recusal is required unless the full court grants the petition. The original judge shall not participate in the merits of the case pending final determination by the full court.

If both parties consent to waive disqualification, they shall file a written stipulation with the court within seven days after notice of the conflict. The stipulation must expressly state that each party knowingly and voluntarily waives any right to challenge the judge’s impartiality. Upon filing, the judge may continue to preside over the proceedings unless the court determines that continued service would compromise judicial integrity or fairness.

On motion for telephone appearance by an incarcerated party, the court shall issue an order directing the facility warden to facilitate participation. The moving party must serve the order on the warden at least fourteen days before the scheduled conference. Service shall also be made on all other parties and the Department of Corrections liaison officer. Failure to provide timely notice may result in denial of the request or rescheduling of the proceeding.

A civil action is commenced by filing a complaint with the court or serving it upon the defendant. If service is made, the plaintiff must file proof of service within fourteen days after service. Failure to serve within ninety-three days after filing requires dismissal without prejudice on motion of any party or on the court’s own initiative.

Service of process is complete upon proof of service at one address. Issuing multiple copies does not toll the ninety-day period. A party seeking extension must file a motion before expiration. The court may grant relief for good cause shown, including diligent efforts to serve. Failure to obtain an extension prior to deadline results in dismissal without prejudice.

Failure to file proof of service does not require dismissal if the party demonstrates good cause for the omission. Upon motion, the court may permit late filing or extend time limits. The moving party must show that the failure was not due to bad faith and that no prejudice results to opposing parties. The court shall grant relief only upon a showing of excusable neglect.

Service upon a person committed to a state psychiatric facility shall be made by delivering a copy of the process to the administrator or other authorized official of the facility. Personal delivery to the defendant is not required. The administrator shall forthwith serve the process on the defendant in accordance with the facility’s regulations and notify the server of the date and manner of service.

If a party is under a disability and has a court-appointed fiduciary, service of process shall be made upon that fiduciary. Service on the fiduciary constitutes valid service on the protected person. If no fiduciary has been appointed, service shall be made as provided for minors or incapacitated persons without representation.

A newspaper qualifies as a paper of general circulation if it has been published at least once every seven days in the county for three consecutive years. Subscriber status is irrelevant. Upon motion, the court shall determine eligibility based on continuous publication history. A party must publish notice in an eligible paper within ten days of the order.

A party may serve documents electronically by transmitting a notification containing a link to a secure online system where the documents are stored, provided the recipient has consented in writing to this method of service. The transmission constitutes service when the notification is sent. The court may order alternative methods if electronic access is unavailable or unreliable.

A stipulation authorizing service by electronic transmission shall specify any file size limitations applicable to the exchanged documents. If no limitation is specified, files exceeding five megabytes shall not be served via text message unless the receiving party consents in writing. Failure to adhere to agreed-upon size constraints renders such service ineffective until cured.

Electronic filings must be submitted in Portable Document Format (PDF) to ensure document integrity and prevent unauthorized alteration. Filings in other formats are prohibited unless the court grants leave on motion for good cause shown. Parties shall verify that electronic submissions remain unaltered from the original filed version.

When serving by direct email or text message pursuant to agreement, the sender must include in the subject line or at the beginning of the message the case name, docket number, and a brief description of the document served. This requirement applies regardless of whether the service is made through the electronic filing system or via alternative means authorized by the parties’ stipulation.

Service by backup electronic method is complete upon transmission. If transmission occurs after 5:00 p.m., or on a Saturday, Sunday, or legal holiday, service is deemed made on the next business day. For deadline purposes, the period begins to run on the day following deemed service.

If a default judgment has been entered, a party seeking to extend the time for filing a motion must comply with the procedures governing relief from judgment. The court may grant an extension only upon a showing of good cause and within the period prescribed for vacating or modifying the judgment. Failure to adhere to those specific requirements shall result in denial of the request.

On motion of the defendant, the court may order the plaintiff to post security for costs. The motion must be filed within 21 days after service of the complaint or within 21 days after the court orders the plaintiff to proceed, whichever is later. The court shall set the amount of security it deems necessary to ensure payment of costs if the plaintiff fails to prevail.

The court may, on motion or sua sponte, permit amendment of pleadings to correct mislabeled counterclaims or cross-claims if justice so requires. Such amendments shall be freely allowed when no prejudice results. Failure to properly designate a claim does not waive its assertion. The court must ensure all substantive issues are adjudicated on their merits rather than dismissed for technical labeling errors.

A party may set forth two or more statements of a claim or defense alternatively or hypothhetically, even if inconsistent. If a party relies on separate occurrences as alternative grounds for a claim or defense, the party may state them separately or alternatively. A party need not adopt a single theory when facts are uncertain.

A party asserting an affirmative defense shall state it in the responsive pleading. Failure to plead an affirmative defense constitutes a waiver, except that the court may, on motion, permit amendment if justice so requires. An affirmative defense includes any matter constituting a bar to recovery, including matters defeating damages, which must be affirmatively pleaded rather than denied.

A plaintiff suing a local government for constitutional violations must attach copies of all relevant local enactments to the complaint. The complaint shall contain short and plain statements detailing the factual basis of the claim, including specific instances of cost-shifting. Failure to include these attachments or sufficient factual detail may result in dismissal without prejudice upon motion by the defendant within twenty-one days after service.

If a party fails to amend within 14 days after service of a motion alleging insufficient clarity, the moving party may seek appropriate relief. On motion, the court shall order the pleading amended or stricken if the defects persist and prejudice the opposing party’s ability to respond with specificity.

A party opposing a motion for summary disposition shall file a response brief and supporting affidavits within twenty-one days after service of the motion, unless the court orders otherwise on motion or stipulation. The moving party may file a reply brief within seven days after service of the opposition materials. Failure to timely file constitutes a waiver of the right to oppose the motion.

An order granting partial dismissal is immediately appealable only if it expressly determines rights and liabilities of fewer than all parties and contains a certification that there is no just reason for delay in appealing. Absent such certification, the order shall not be appealed until entry of final judgment disposing of all claims against all parties.

A party filing a document in paper format shall affix a flag to the first page. The flag must be clearly visible and identify the case name, docket number, and nature of the document. Handwritten identification on the cover page is insufficient unless the court orders otherwise. Failure to comply may result in rejection of the filing.

A party seeking reconsideration of an order denying a motion to strike must file a request for the court to take another look within fourteen days after entry of the order. The request shall state specific grounds for relief and may be granted only if new evidence or controlling legal authority has become available since the prior ruling.

In an action against a public body or the state, a party may name the office rather than the incumbent. When suing a government official in an official capacity, the complaint shall designate the defendant by title or office. The court may order substitution of the successor if the named official leaves office during pendency of the action.

On motion of a party asserting that a person who is not a party has become the owner or successor in interest of the claim, the court may order that person to be substituted as a party. The motion must be filed within 30 days after the transfer occurs. If the motion is not timely made, the action proceeds as if no transfer had occurred.

A party may serve a complaint against a nonparty or co-defendant for indemnity or contribution arising from the same transaction or occurrence. The third-party complaint must be served within 14 days after serving the answer, unless the court permits later service. Leave of court is required if service occurs more than 14 days after the answer.

On motion by any party, the court may permit persons to join as plaintiffs if they assert rights arising out of the same transaction, occurrence, or series of transactions or occurrences, and if any question of law or fact common to all plaintiffs will arise in the action. The court shall state its reasons for denying joinder.

A plaintiff may join persons as defendants if any question of law or fact common to all defendants arises out of the same transaction, occurrence, or series of transactions or occurrences, and if any relief is sought against them jointly, severally, or in the alternative. The court may order separate trials or make other orders to avoid prejudice or confusion.

On motion of any party or on its own initiative, the court may at any stage in the action add or delete a party. The court shall grant leave to amend the pleading to effect such addition or deletion unless substantial prejudice results. A motion to delete a party must be served on all parties.

If a statute’s constitutionality is challenged, the court may order any party to serve notice on the Attorney General within ten days. The notice must specify the nature of the challenge and identify the statute. Failure to comply may result in sanctions. The court shall determine whether notice is necessary based on the interests of justice and public policy.

On motion of any party, the court may transfer an action involving personal injury to another county if venue is improper or for convenience of parties and witnesses. The motion must be filed within thirty days after service of the complaint. The court shall order transfer upon finding that justice requires it.

If the court determines it lacks subject-matter jurisdiction sua sponte, it shall not transfer the case until each party has had an opportunity to be heard on the issue. The court must provide reasonable notice of its intent to dismiss or transfer and allow parties to file written objections within ten days before entering any order redirecting the file to a proper tribunal.

On motion by any party or on its own initiative, the court may transfer a case to the Court of Claims at any time if jurisdiction is lacking. A motion seeking transfer after the initial response deadline must demonstrate good cause for the delay. The court shall grant leave to file such a late motion upon finding that the interest of justice requires transfer and no substantial prejudice will result from the delay.

A motion to compel discovery shall be filed before the expiration of the discovery cutoff date. A motion filed after such date is prohibited unless the court, on motion and for good cause shown, grants leave to file. The court may impose terms as a condition of granting relief. Failure to timely move constitutes waiver of the right to compel.

A party claiming damages for in-home care or daily-living assistance shall disclose the names of individuals who provided such services within thirty days after service of a request for disclosure. Failure to provide these names constitutes a waiver of evidence regarding those specific services, unless good cause is shown. The court may impose sanctions for noncompliance.

A party must serve initial disclosures on any person or party joining the action after the initial disclosures have been served. Service shall be made within fourteen days after service of a pleading, motion, notice, or other paper that adds the new party to the action. Failure to make timely service does not affect the validity of the initial disclosures previously served.

A party joined after the deadline for initial disclosures must serve its disclosure statement within fourteen days after being served with a pleading or order adding it as a party, unless the court orders otherwise on motion for good cause shown. This time period may be shortened or extended by stipulation of the parties or by court order.

On motion for discovery of non-party consultant files, the court may grant access only if the moving party demonstrates substantial need and that such material cannot be obtained with undue hardship by other means. Any order granting discovery shall impose conditions protecting against disclosure of confidential information not reasonably available from other sources.

A party may obtain discovery regarding an opposing expert’s opinions or data if the proponent demonstrates to the court that equivalent information is not reasonably available from other sources. The court shall grant such discovery only upon a finding of good cause and subject to protective orders necessary to prevent undue burden or prejudice.

Before serving discovery requests, an attorney must certify that they are not interposed for any improper purpose, including to harass or cause unnecessary delay or needless expense. The certification shall be signed by at least one attorney of record in the attorney’s own name, stating the date and place of execution.

On motion for permission to take a deposition before action, the movant must serve the motion and notice of hearing on every person to be deposed and all other parties known to have an interest in the subject matter. Service must occur at least 14 days before the hearing date. The court may shorten or extend this time for good cause shown.

A party may take the deposition of any person, including an adverse party, without leave of court. However, no party shall serve a notice to take a deposition upon a defendant until after service of the summons and complaint has been completed. This requirement does not apply if the defendant has already made an appearance in the action or if the parties agree otherwise in writing.

Upon designation of an organization, the requesting party shall specify the matters for examination. The organization must designate representatives within 14 days. Objections to designations must be filed within seven days after service of the designation. Each designated representative’s deposition is limited to one day of seven hours, unless otherwise ordered by the court or stipulated by the parties.

The officer before whom the deposition is taken shall administer an oath to the deponent before taking testimony. The attorney noticing the deposition must ensure that a qualified officer is present to administer the oath. Failure to administer the oath renders the deposition inadmissible unless waived by all parties or ordered by the court for good cause shown.

The party noticing the deposition shall arrange for a court reporter or other qualified person to record the testimony verbatim. The recording officer may delegate transcription duties to another individual provided the officer personally supervises the process and certifies the accuracy of the final transcript. Failure to comply renders the deposition inadmissible unless the court orders otherwise on motion showing good cause.

A party may instruct a deponent to answer a question only if the instruction is in good faith and asserts a privilege, seeks to enforce a court limitation, or presents an objection to evidence admissibility under MRE 408. The instruction must be concise and nonargumentative. Failure to comply with this requirement constitutes grounds for the court to impose sanctions upon motion by any party.

A party responding to a request for production may respond that inspection of documents is available upon reasonable notice. If the responding party elects this method, it shall specify the location of the documents with sufficient particularity to permit identification and inspection. The requesting party must bear the cost of copying unless otherwise ordered by the court or agreed by the parties.

On motion showing good cause, the court may order a party to submit to a physical or mental examination by a licensed examiner. The order shall specify the time, place, manner, conditions, and scope of the examination, as well as the person or persons who shall perform it. The moving party must serve notice on all parties at least 14 days before the hearing date.

A party challenging the sufficiency of a response to a request for admission must first confer in good faith with the responding party to resolve the dispute. If unresolved, the moving party may file a motion. The court shall determine the sufficiency of the response and order costs or sanctions as appropriate.

Any request to modify dates established by a scheduling order shall be made by motion. The moving party must justify the requested alteration by demonstrating good cause or manifest injustice. The court may grant such relief only if the justification satisfies the statutory requirements for modification. Failure to provide adequate justification shall result in denial of the motion without further hearing.

The court shall conduct a pretrial conference to resolve disputes regarding the admissibility of recorded expert testimony. Parties must stipulate to specific segments for jury presentation or file objections within fourteen days. The court shall determine which portions are admitted, excluding irrelevant or prejudicial material. This process ensures only agreed-upon or judicially approved testimony is presented at trial.

On motion of any party, the court may exclude from evidence or bar the testimony of any witness not included in the pretrial witness list. The court shall grant such relief unless the moving party demonstrates good cause for the failure to disclose or that the opposing party suffered prejudice. The court may permit amendment of the list on just terms.

Parties must meet and confer to discuss discovery matters, including whether the costs of retrieving electronically stored information shall be shared. This discussion must occur within thirty days after service of the initial pleading or earlier as ordered by the court. Parties shall prepare a written statement of any agreements reached or issues remaining unresolved for submission to the court upon request or motion.

The proposal shall include a concise statement of the nature of the action and a summary of the relevant background facts sufficient to inform the court of the context for discovery. This statement must be included in the initial electronic discovery plan filed within thirty days after the first pretrial conference, unless the court orders otherwise on motion or sua sponte.

A party may appear by telephone or other electronic means if the court permits. Appearance via video conference with audio enabled constitutes a telephone appearance regardless of whether the camera is activated, provided the party can be heard clearly and participates fully in the proceeding. The court may require video activation at its discretion.

When a case is referred to another county for alternative dispute resolution under an intercounty agreement, the referring court shall not assess administrative fees against the parties. The receiving court may charge reasonable costs directly related to the ADR process. Any such charges must be approved by the referring court prior to referral and shall be borne equally by the parties unless otherwise ordered.

If technical difficulties prevent effective participation, the court may require physical appearance. A party whose remote connection fails must appear in person within twenty-four hours unless excused for good cause. Opposing counsel may continue remote appearance if their connection remains stable. Failure to comply with an order to appear in person constitutes default.

The court shall permit a detained defendant to appear by video communication if the sheriff certifies that transport poses a significant security risk or logistical burden. Upon such certification, the court must order remote appearance unless it finds that physical presence is essential for the fairness of the proceeding. The party seeking in-person appearance bears the burden of demonstrating prejudice resulting from remote participation.

The ADR clerk shall serve copies of the mediation order on all parties and the neutral within three days after entry. The neutral shall contact counsel to schedule sessions, considering pending discovery needs. Sessions must be scheduled within thirty days unless the court orders otherwise for good cause shown.

An entity seeking approval as a settlement facilitator must submit credentials and the required application forms to the circuit court administrator. Applications shall be filed within thirty days of the request for approval. The court may approve or deny the application based on compliance with established standards. Approved entities must maintain current certification records accessible upon request by the court clerk.

An approved mediator shall remain on the general civil mediation roster for a term of three years. Upon expiration of the term, the mediator must file a new application for approval to continue serving. The court may extend a mediator’s term upon motion and for good cause shown. Failure to reapply within thirty days after expiration results in removal from the roster.

If the clerk denies an application for assignment to the general civil roster, the applicant may file a motion with the chief judge within fourteen days of denial. The court shall rule on the motion without a hearing unless the chief judge determines that oral argument is necessary in the interest of justice.

Upon filing notice of bankruptcy, the court shall stay proceedings until the automatic stay terminates or is lifted. A party may move to lift the stay or revive the action. The court shall grant relief from the stay if the federal bankruptcy court determines that the state proceeding does not interfere with the bankruptcy estate.

On motion of any party, if scheduling conflicts between trials in different courts cannot be resolved by agreement, the presiding judges shall confer to resolve the conflict. If unresolved, either judge may refer the matter to the Chief Judge of the Administrative District for assignment or rescheduling. The referral must occur within five days after the failure to reach an agreement.

If the court declines to terminate an action for lack of prosecution, it shall issue an order setting forth specific conditions for further proceedings. The order must designate a date by which the parties shall complete discovery or file motions. Failure to comply with the order’s directives within the prescribed time may result in dismissal of the action or entry of default judgment against the non-complying party.

On motion or sua sponte, the court shall order separate trials of claims, crossclaims, counterclaims, third-party claims, or particular issues if necessary to avoid prejudice, confusion, delay, or expense. The court may bifurcate any issue for trial before a jury when evidence admissible on one issue is prejudicial to another and inadmissible on that other issue.

A jury demand filed in district court remains effective upon transfer to circuit court. No additional filing fee is required for the jury demand in circuit court if the demand was timely filed in district court. The party need not pay any difference in jury fees between the courts. Failure to file a new demand in circuit court does not constitute a waiver of the right to a jury trial.

On motion or sua sponte, the court may order separate trials of legal and equitable claims to promote convenience, avoid prejudice, or save time. The court shall determine the sequence of issues. Any order must preserve a party’s right to a jury trial on legal demands. The court may require one issue to be tried before another, provided no right to a jury determination is waived by the sequencing.

The jury coordinator shall notify prospective jurors by first-class mail at least fourteen days before the scheduled date for voir dire. Telephone notification is prohibited for initial contact unless the court, on motion or sua sponte, finds that mailing is impracticable and orders alternative notice methods consistent with due process requirements.

The committee shall publish proposed instructions for public comment at least thirty days before adoption. Publication must include the text of each new or revised instruction and a statement of reasons for the change. The committee shall provide notice to all interested parties and post the materials on its official website. No instruction may be adopted until the comment period expires and the committee considers all received comments.

A party waives the right to have an issue decided by the jury if that issue is omitted from the special verdict form and no objection is made before the jury begins deliberations. Failure to object prior to deliberation constitutes a waiver of the right to submit that specific factual question to the trier of fact, regardless of whether the omission was inadvertent or intentional.

Within fourteen days after entry of judgment, a party may file a motion to amend or make additional findings of fact. The motion must state with particularity the facts sought to be amended or added and the grounds therefor. The court may grant leave to amend or make additional findings if new evidence is offered or if the findings are clearly erroneous.

A party objecting to a proposed order shall serve copies of the objections on all other parties within 14 days after service of the proposed order. The objections must state with particularity the grounds for objection and identify the specific provisions objected to. Failure to include these requirements constitutes a waiver of the right to object.

A party objecting to the proposed judgment shall file written objections with the court within fourteen days after service of the affidavit. If no objection is filed within that period, the court may enter judgment in accordance with the settlement agreement without further hearing or notice. Failure to object constitutes a waiver of any defense regarding the accuracy of the affidavit or the terms of the agreement.

The clerk shall mail notice of entry of default to any party who has not filed an appearance or other pleading in the action. Notice must be sent within seven days after the default is entered. Failure to provide such notice does not invalidate the default, but the court may set aside the default on motion for good cause shown if prejudice results from the lack of notice.

Within seven days after entry of default judgment, the prevailing party shall serve a copy on the adverse party or counsel. Proof of service must be filed with the court within fourteen days after entry. Failure to comply may result in vacation of the judgment on motion for good cause shown. The court may extend time upon application demonstrating diligence.

In an action seeking declaratory relief, a party may demand a jury trial by serving a written demand on all other parties within twenty-one days after service of the last pleading directed to the issue. Failure to serve such demand constitutes a waiver. The court shall try any issue so demanded by a jury unless the right is waived or the court determines that no right to a jury trial exists under applicable law.

On motion of a defendant who was served but did not receive actual notice of the action, the court shall set aside a default entered against that defendant if the motion is filed within one year after entry of the default. The court may impose conditions necessary to protect the plaintiff’s interests and ensure just resolution of the controversy.

If the judge who issued an order is absent or unavailable, any other judge with jurisdiction over the case may, on motion and for good cause shown, stay enforcement of that order pending a hearing. The moving party must file the motion within seven days after learning of the absence. The substitute judge shall rule promptly to prevent irreparable harm.

A warrant issued by a Native American tribal court shall be recognized and enforced in Michigan courts of record with the same effect as if issued by a Michigan court. A party seeking enforcement must file a certified copy of the warrant within ten days of arrest. The court may modify procedures on motion for good cause shown, ensuring due process rights are preserved while honoring intergovernmental comity obligations.

On motion without notice, a party may seek an order compelling further post-judgment discovery. The court shall grant relief only if the movant demonstrates good cause for additional examination or that prior proceedings were insufficient to satisfy the judgment. The court may impose conditions necessary to prevent harassment or undue burden on the debtor.

The bill of costs shall include the name, address, telephone number, and email address of opposing counsel and any self-represented parties. This information must be provided to facilitate service and communication regarding the cost award. Failure to include such directory information may result in the court striking the bill or delaying consideration until compliance is achieved.

For purposes of this rule, “foster-care placement” includes any twenty-four-hour substitute care for a child whose parents lack legal custody, including placement with a relative serving as court-appointed legal caretaker. This definition applies regardless of whether parental rights remain intact or have been permanently severed.

Upon satisfaction of the judgment in full, the judgment creditor shall file a certificate of satisfaction with the clerk within ten days. A copy of the certificate shall be served on the judgment debtor and any garnishee holding funds or wages. Upon filing, the court shall issue an order discharging all pending garnishments and stays of execution related to the satisfied judgment.

The garnishee shall state in the answer whether another writ of garnishment is pending against the garnishee. If so, the answer must specify the court, case number, and date of issuance of that prior writ. The garnishee shall also disclose the amount withheld under the prior order and the remaining balance due to the judgment debtor.

On motion, the court may grant prejudgment attachment if the plaintiff shows probable cause that the defendant owes a fixed sum under an agreement, exclusive of any counterclaim or setoff. The moving party must file an affidavit setting forth facts establishing this debt and demonstrating that the amount exceeds any defenses asserted by the debtor.

Upon motion to dissolve prejudgment seizure, the court shall set a hearing within seven days. The moving party may request subpoenas for witnesses attending the hearing. The court shall issue such subpoenas upon application, provided the applicant identifies the witnesses and the expected testimony. Failure to appear by subpoenaed witnesses does not delay the hearing unless good cause is shown.

A party opposing an installment payment order must file a written response within fourteen days after service of the motion. If no response is filed, the court may grant the motion without further notice. Upon timely filing, the court shall schedule a hearing on the matter and notify all parties of the date and time for appearance.

On motion for judgment against shareholders, the court shall order the corporation’s registered agent to produce a current shareholder roster within ten days. The agent must submit an affidavit verifying the roster’s accuracy as of the production date. Failure to comply subjects the agent to contempt sanctions. The court may impose additional conditions necessary to ensure complete disclosure of ownership interests.

In an action involving a person alleged to be incapacitated, that person shall be sued by naming the guardian ad litem or conservator, if appointed. If no guardian or conservator has been appointed, the party seeking relief must file a motion for appointment of a guardian ad litem before proceeding with substantive claims. The court may appoint a guardian ad litem on its own initiative or upon application.

Upon filing of any document affecting custody or support, the clerk shall promptly transmit a copy to the Friend of the Court office. This duty applies unless the court orders otherwise or the parties have agreed in writing that the Friend of the Court is not involved. Transmission must occur within three business days of filing.

Upon entry of a new order involving a subsequent child, the court shall incorporate by reference any active prior orders concerning other children. To modify terms for a previously adjudicated child within the same proceeding, the moving party must file a separate motion demonstrating changed circumstances or best interests, and the court shall hold an evidentiary hearing before altering existing custody or support arrangements.

On motion, the court may order a party to advance funds for discovery expenses if the moving party demonstrates an inability to pay such costs. The motion must include an affidavit detailing the party’s financial status and the specific discovery sought. The court shall grant the order only upon finding that the opposing party has the ability to pay and that the requested discovery is necessary for the just determination of the action.

If a party’s conduct causes the loss of federal Title IV-D funding eligibility for a case, the Friend of the Court shall suspend performance of its statutory duties regarding that case. The suspension continues until funding eligibility is restored or the court orders otherwise. A party may move to reinstate services upon demonstrating restoration of eligibility.

Upon entry of default, the prevailing party shall serve notice of the entry upon all other parties within three days. Within seven days after service, the prevailing party shall file proof of service with the clerk. Failure to provide timely notice may result in setting aside the default. The court may extend these time periods for good cause shown.

Upon objection to a proposed relocation, the court shall schedule an evidentiary hearing within thirty days of filing the objection. The court may extend this period for good cause shown. Testimony regarding the best interests of the child must be taken at such hearing. Failure to object timely waives the right to contest the relocation.

The judgment shall specify the party with whom the child resides, the other parent’s parenting time schedule, and provisions for decision-making authority. The court shall include terms addressing transportation responsibilities, holiday alternation, and methods for resolving future disputes regarding custody or parenting time. These mandatory provisions must be clearly stated within the operative text of the final order.

On motion by either party, the court may modify or extinguish an assigned arrearage balance upon a final judgment of support modification. The moving party must demonstrate that strict enforcement would cause undue hardship and is contrary to the best interests of the child. The court shall consider the assignee’s interest only if the state consents to the reduction.

Upon transfer of a domestic relations case to circuit court, the clerk shall not require payment of new-case costs before hearing an emergency motion. The court may hear such motions immediately upon filing, regardless of whether the plaintiff has paid the required fees. Failure to pay costs shall not delay consideration of matters requiring urgent judicial intervention to prevent irreparable harm.

The applicant shall indicate willingness to make recommendations regarding custody and support matters. The applicant shall state the hourly fee charged for mediation services. This information must be included in the application submitted to the circuit court clerk within thirty days of appointment or designation as a domestic relations mediator, unless the court orders otherwise.

On motion of any party, the court may order genetic testing at any time before final judgment, notwithstanding failure to request such testing at pretrial.
