The court shall grant the motion if it finds that justice requires testing and that the delay did not prejudice the opposing party’s ability to prepare for trial.

Upon issuance of a bench warrant for contempt, the court shall hold a hearing to determine compliance within fourteen days of the respondent’s arrest or voluntary appearance. If the hearing is not held within this period, the warrant expires and the respondent must be released from custody immediately, unless the court finds good cause for delay and orders continued detention pending a rescheduled hearing.

On motion by any party, the court may waive the six-month waiting period required for entry of judgment in a consent decree proceeding if the parties demonstrate that immediate entry serves the interests of justice. The motion must be filed with the complaint or answer and state specific facts justifying the waiver.

On motion by any party, the court may order joint sessions despite prior objection to alternative dispute resolution. Such an order shall be issued only upon a finding that individual sessions have failed to resolve disputed issues or that joint participation is necessary for effective mediation. The moving party must file the motion within ten days after the initial assessment conference.

Mediation is prohibited if domestic violence exists unless the victim consents in writing. The mediator shall assess for intimidation or abuse before commencing and periodically during mediation. If intimidation or abuse occurs, the mediator must terminate proceedings immediately. Participation remains voluntary; no party may be compelled to mediate against their will.

Before mediation commences, the friend of the court shall conduct a screening for domestic violence using the standardized assessment form prescribed by the State Court Administrative Office. If the screening indicates a risk of abuse, the parties shall not engage in joint mediation sessions unless the court determines that safety measures are sufficient to protect all participants.

The facilitator shall explain the contents of the post-meeting report to the parties. The facilitator shall inform the parties that they may file objections within twenty-one days after receiving the report. This briefing requirement applies unless the court orders otherwise or the parties waive this right in writing.

The caption must identify the underlying case. The moving party shall serve the motion for superintending control on all parties to the underlying action within seven days after filing. Service constitutes notice. If no underlying case exists, service is required only on adverse parties. The court may shorten or extend these time periods for good cause shown.

A writ of habeas corpus challenging the custody of a defendant detained in county jail pending trial shall be issued only by the circuit court having jurisdiction over the underlying criminal charges. No other court may issue such a writ for a pretrial detainee. The application must be filed in the appropriate circuit court, regardless of the location of the detention facility.

On motion, the court may order an incarcerated person transferred from confinement to appear at a hearing. If the custodian lacks personnel for direct escort, the custodian shall deliver the person to authorized law enforcement or transport deputies designated by the court. Such delivery must occur within forty-eight hours of the order, ensuring secure custody throughout transit until arrival at the specified location.

On an ex parte motion demonstrating immediate irreparable harm, the court may issue an initial order without notice. The order shall specify the date by which the respondent must file a response. This deadline shall be no fewer than three days after service of the order, unless good cause is shown for a shorter period.

In an action to oust persons holding themselves out as corporations without authority, the Attorney General shall name the respondents as "persons acting under color of corporate authority." The complaint must allege specific facts demonstrating unauthorized use of a corporate name or structure. Failure to identify respondents within this statutory category renders the pleading subject to dismissal for failure to state a claim upon which relief can be granted.

On motion by the Attorney General in any quo warranto proceeding, the court may order the relator to post security for costs. The order shall specify the amount and form of security required. Failure to comply within ten days after service of the order constitutes grounds for dismissal of the information without prejudice.

On motion for temporary restraining order without notice, movant shall file an affidavit stating efforts to notify opposing counsel and reasons why notice was impracticable. If no effort was made, the affidavit shall state reasons therefor. The court may require movant to give immediate notice upon issuance of the order.

In an action for partition of real property, if a party joins a mortgagee as a necessary party, the initial pleading must allege the existence of the mortgage, identify the recording data, and state the unpaid principal balance. Failure to include these allegations constitutes a defect in form that may be cured by amendment within twenty-one days after service of a motion to strike or for more definite statement.

On motion of any party, the court may partition real property interests held by unidentified heirs or devisees. The court shall order the specific share set apart and sold, with proceeds deposited into a separate interest-bearing account pending identification of rightful owners. This action is subject to adequate notice to all known parties and proof that reasonable efforts to locate current holders have failed.

On motion for sale in lieu of partition, the petitioner shall deposit with the court clerk any proceeds attributable to missing heirs or out-of-state life tenants. This deposit must occur within fourteen days after entry of the order of sale. The funds shall remain held by the clerk, subject to further court order, until all interested parties are located or their interests are otherwise determined by law.

On motion of any party entitled to distribution, the court shall order payment of sale proceeds held by the clerk. If an interest is encumbered, the court shall direct payment to the lienholder or require satisfaction of the encumbrance before distributing the balance to the owner. The motion must be filed within 30 days after the clerk deposits the funds.

The moving party shall file an affidavit proving service of notice upon all lienholders. Service is satisfied by mailing copies to each holder at their last known address or by personal delivery. The affidavit must list every lienholder notified and the method used. Failure to provide such proof constitutes grounds for denying the motion for partition sale.

A party seeking to extend the time for filing a motion for class certification must file a separate written motion demonstrating good cause. An agreement between counsel is insufficient to toll or extend the deadline. The court may grant an extension only upon finding that strict compliance would result in manifest injustice and that the moving party has acted with due diligence.

The notice shall identify each lead plaintiff by name and residence. It must state whether any lead plaintiff has been convicted of a felony or committed acts involving fraud, dishonesty, or breach of trust. This disclosure is required to inform class members of potential conflicts of interest affecting the adequacy of representation. The court may order additional disclosures necessary to ensure fair notice under all circumstances.

The parties may stipulate to a settlement agreement notwithstanding the absence of residual funds for distribution. Such stipulation shall be filed with the court and served upon all class members within fourteen days of execution. The court shall approve the settlement only if it finds the agreement fair, reasonable, and adequate under the circumstances, ensuring that the interests of absent class members are protected despite the lack of remaining assets.

If a judgment or order is silent regarding unclaimed funds in a class action settlement, the court shall order distribution to cy pres beneficiaries. A party must file a motion proposing such distribution within thirty days after the claims administration period expires. The court may approve the proposal if it finds the proposed recipients are reasonably related to the interests furthered by the underlying litigation and that the distribution serves the public interest.

In a shareholder derivative action, the complaint must allege with particularity the plaintiff’s efforts to secure appropriate action from the directors or explain why such efforts were not made. Failure to include these allegations constitutes grounds for dismissal of the complaint without prejudice, unless the court grants leave to amend.

Upon granting a motion to compel arbitration, the court shall stay all proceedings in the action pending resolution of the dispute through arbitration. The stay remains in effect until the arbitrator issues a final award or the court vacates the arbitration agreement. A party may move to lift the stay only upon demonstrating that arbitration is no longer feasible or has been completed.

On motion of any party, the court may order joint trials of two or more actions if they arise from the same transaction or series of transactions, even though the claims are unrelated. This rule applies when separate suits involve common questions of law or fact and joinder prevents inconsistent verdicts or duplicative litigation regarding identical relief sought against a single defendant.

On motion for forfeiture, the moving party shall serve notice upon the surety at the address designated in the undertaking. Service is complete upon mailing to that last known address. Proof of service must be filed within ten days after filing the motion. Failure to serve does not preclude entry of judgment if the court finds actual notice was received or service was reasonably attempted.

If corporate records are unavailable, the petitioner shall estimate paid-in capital based on the best available evidence. The court may require an independent appraisal if the estimate is contested. The petitioner must file supporting documentation within fourteen days of the petition’s filing. Failure to provide adequate proof may result in dismissal without prejudice.

The petitioner shall file proof of publication within fourteen days after the final publication date. Proof must consist of an affidavit by the publisher or a printed copy of the notice, showing the date and place of publication. Failure to file timely proof constitutes grounds for dismissal of the petition without prejudice. The court may extend time for good cause shown on motion.

In parental rights restoration proceedings, the court shall omit the youth’s name from the case caption, substituting “Youth” or initials. Confidential contact information for the youth must be filed separately under seal. Parties shall not disclose such details in public filings. The clerk shall maintain these records confidentially, accessible only to authorized personnel and parties with proper standing, ensuring the youth’s identity remains protected throughout the proceeding.

A party failing to provide a social security number in an emancipation petition may amend the pleading to include such number. The amendment shall be filed within fourteen days after the hearing date, on motion or with leave of court. The court may impose conditions necessary to ensure accuracy and prevent prejudice to any interested party.

A party may file a motion for a personal protection order in a pending domestic relations action. The motion shall be filed within thirty days of the occurrence necessitating relief or upon showing good cause for delay. The court may grant the order if it finds immediate and irreparable injury, loss, or damage will result if the order is not granted.

On motion of the petitioner or stipulation of all parties, the court shall dismiss the petition without prejudice. No filing fee shall be charged for such dismissal. The order dismissing the petition must be entered within seven days after the motion is filed or the stipulation is submitted to the court.

Upon application by law enforcement showing probable cause that respondent failed to surrender firearms within forty-eight hours of service, the court shall issue a warrant authorizing search for and seizure of such weapons. The affidavit must allege specific facts demonstrating noncompliance with the order’s firearm surrender provisions.

On motion by law enforcement showing probable cause that firearms or concealed pistol licenses are located at specific premises, the court shall issue an order authorizing entry and seizure. The court must grant the request if sufficient evidence demonstrates the items’ presence. Officers shall execute the order immediately upon issuance to secure dangerous weapons and prevent imminent harm to public safety.

If the respondent fails to appear at the hearing on the order to show cause, the court shall issue a warrant for the respondent’s arrest. The court may not exercise discretion to dismiss the proceedings or set a new hearing date without an appearance. The warrant remains in effect until the respondent is brought before the court or released pursuant to law.

In an adoption proceeding involving an Indian child, the court shall treat the child’s tribe, the Bureau of Indian Affairs, and any other interested party designated by the tribe as interested persons. If the child’s tribal affiliation cannot be determined, the Bureau of Indian Affairs shall be treated as an interested person. The court must notify these parties within 30 days after determining that the ICWA applies to the proceeding.

If the child is eligible for membership in an Indian tribe, the court shall order notice to the biological father of any adoption proceeding, regardless of his acknowledgment of paternity. Notice must be served within ten days after the filing of the petition. This requirement applies unless the father has previously waived his right to notice in writing before a judge.

If the biological parent or Indian tribe cannot be located, notice of subsequent hearings shall be given by certified mail to the Bureau of Indian Affairs and any known tribal representatives. This notice must be sent within ten days before the hearing date. Failure to locate a party does not relieve the petitioner of the duty to provide such notice to the Bureau.

The court shall verify that the parent understands the consequences of relinquishment before accepting consent. Consent is invalid if executed within thirty days of birth or prior to twenty days post-delivery, unless exigent circumstances exist. The judge must ensure compliance with federal Indian Child Welfare Act standards regarding voluntary surrender and informed consent procedures.

On motion to transfer jurisdiction to an Indian tribe, the court shall grant the transfer unless clear and convincing evidence demonstrates that the tribal court lacks jurisdiction or that the tribe’s social services are inadequate. Allegations of inadequacy alone do not constitute grounds for denial. The moving party must file the motion within 14 days after receiving notice of the pendency of proceedings.

Upon entry of an order terminating parental rights, the court shall notify the terminated parent that the obligation to pay child support continues until adoption or emancipation. This notice must be provided in writing at the time of the hearing or within ten days thereafter. Failure to provide such notice does not extinguish the support obligation but may affect enforcement remedies.

“Legal custody” means authority over a child under the Juvenile Code. This designation is distinct from an EPIC guardianship. A party seeking legal custody must file a motion specifying the basis for relief. The court shall determine custody based on the child’s best interests. Orders granting legal custody do not confer rights equivalent to those established under the Estates and Protected Individuals Code unless expressly stated.

An affidavit of parentage must be executed before an officer authorized to administer oaths. Upon execution, the document shall be filed with the Register of Vital Records within ten days. Failure to file within this period renders the affidavit void unless the court orders otherwise on motion for good cause shown. The parties bear responsibility for ensuring proper notarization and timely submission.

On motion of a party or sua sponte, the court may issue an interim custody order removing a minor from a guardian’s possession pending final disposition if clear and convincing evidence demonstrates immediate danger to the child’s physical safety or welfare. Such order shall specify conditions for visitation and support, remain in effect until modified or vacated by further order, and be entered within five days of the hearing.

The placement plan must include transition and post-release support services for a period of not less than ninety days following discharge from the qualified residential treatment program. This requirement applies unless the court finds, based on clear and convincing evidence, that such duration is unnecessary to ensure the juvenile’s safety and successful reintegration into the community.

If the court grants additional peremptory challenges to multiple respondents due to separate interests, it must grant an equal number of additional peremptory challenges to the petitioner. The total number of peremptory challenges granted to any party shall not exceed the statutory maximum applicable to that proceeding.

In a designated case, the judge conducting the probable-cause hearing may accept a guilty plea but is disqualified from presiding at trial. Upon motion by a party, the court shall assign a different judge for any contested proceeding if the same judge heard the preliminary examination. This disqualification applies unless all parties expressly waive the right to an impartial trial judge in writing on the record.

In child protective proceedings, a nonattorney referee may preside over preliminary hearings, detention hearings, and dispositional hearings. The referee shall not preside over termination of parental rights hearings or any hearing involving contested factual issues requiring evidentiary rulings by a judge. The court must appoint the referee subject to the consent of all parties.

At the initial appearance, the judge shall advise the respondent of the right to be represented by counsel at every stage of the proceedings. If the respondent is unable to obtain counsel, the court shall appoint an attorney. The judge shall ensure the respondent understands these rights before proceeding with any further inquiry or disposition under this chapter.

Upon motion by any party or sua sponte, the court may appoint separate counsel to represent the child’s expressed preferences if such interests conflict with those of the guardian ad litem. Appointment shall occur promptly upon finding a conflict exists. Separate counsel must advocate solely for the child’s stated wishes, distinct from the welfare determination made by the guardian ad litem.

A Court Appointed Special Advocate shall conduct ongoing investigations into the child’s circumstances and submit written reports to the court within thirty days of appointment and thereafter as ordered. These reports must address the child’s safety, permanency, and well-being, including recommendations for placement and services. The advocate shall attend all hearings and cooperate with parties to ensure accurate fact-finding.

The court may order service by first-class mail or other method reasonably calculated to provide notice. Upon such order, the petitioner must serve the initial pleading within ten days after entry of the order. Proof of service must be filed with the clerk within five days after service. Service is complete upon mailing or completion of the alternative method ordered by the court.

If the tribe cannot be identified or located, notice must be sent by registered mail to the Secretary of the Interior. The approved form shall include a statement advising the recipient of the right to petition the court for transfer of jurisdiction to the tribal court and the right to intervene in the proceeding within thirty days of receipt.

The court shall ensure that written notice of the permanency planning hearing is served on all parties at least 14 days before the scheduled date. Notice must include the time, place, and purpose of the hearing. Failure to provide timely notice does not invalidate proceedings if a party waives the requirement in writing or appears without objection.

Within three days after filing a petition, the prosecuting attorney shall serve notice of the proceedings upon all parties, including the child’s court-appointed advocate. Service must be made personally or by certified mail. If the advocate is not yet appointed, notice shall be served upon the agency responsible for appointment. The court may extend this time for good cause shown.

In any proceeding involving a minor, the party initiating the action shall serve notice upon the minor’s legal custodian if the custodian is not a party to the action. Service must occur within ten days after filing the initial pleading or motion, unless the court orders otherwise for good cause shown. Failure to provide such notice may result in dismissal of the proceeding or other sanctions as determined by the court.

In termination proceedings where service by publication is ordered due to unknown residence, the court shall order that the putative father’s name be omitted from the published notice. The notice must identify the party only as “the putative father” or by initials, unless the court finds good cause for full disclosure. This protection applies regardless of prior establishment of paternity.

The petitioner shall serve notice of the hearing upon any putative father within ten days after filing the petition. The notice must state the time, date, and place of the hearing and inform the recipient that he may appear to assert paternity and seek custody or visitation rights. Failure to provide such notice precludes adjudication of parental rights against the putative father unless good cause is shown.

On motion of a party or sua sponte, the court may order an alleged biological father to establish a parent-child relationship within a specified period if facts indicate probable paternity and it serves the child’s best interests. The court shall set the deadline and may extend it for good cause shown. Failure to respond within the prescribed time constitutes waiver of standing.

Before conducting a visual identification of a juvenile defendant, the court shall advise the defendant and the defendant’s parent or guardian that they have the right to counsel for the proceeding. If the defendant is indigent, the court shall appoint counsel if requested. This advice shall be given on the record prior to the identification.

The court shall permit inspection of juvenile protection case files only by parties to the proceeding, their counsel, and individuals expressly authorized by statute or court order. All other persons are prohibited from accessing such records. The court may restrict further access if disclosure would endanger the child’s safety or privacy.

On motion of a party or sua sponte, the court may transfer a designated juvenile case to the county of the defendant’s residence for disposition purposes only. Such transfer shall not affect jurisdiction for trial or sentencing if conviction occurs in the original venue. The receiving court shall conduct disposition proceedings consistent with applicable law.

The prosecutor shall attend the initial case conference. A defendant placed on the consent calendar must complete all program conditions within twelve months of placement, unless the court grants an extension for good cause shown upon motion. Failure to comply may result in revocation of the consent calendar status and resumption of standard criminal proceedings.

The court may transfer any matter from the consent calendar to the formal docket without a hearing if the petition has not been signed or approved. Such transfer is proper upon the court’s determination that further proceedings are necessary to resolve jurisdictional defects, procedural irregularities, or substantive issues requiring formal adjudication. The clerk shall update the docket accordingly.

In a case involving a juvenile charged with a designated major felony, the preliminary examination shall be held within fourteen days after arraignment. This period may be extended by the court for good cause shown. No other delay provisions applicable to adult defendants govern this proceeding. The court must ensure strict compliance with these time limits to protect the juvenile’s right to a speedy determination of probable cause.

On motion of the prosecutor, the court may order transfer to adult criminal jurisdiction if it finds probable cause that the youth committed the offense and that public safety requires such transfer. The motion must be filed before the conclusion of the preliminary hearing. The court shall hold a hearing on the motion, allowing both parties to present evidence and argument regarding the appropriateness of transfer.

Upon completion of risk and mental health screenings, the court shall determine whether to dismiss the case, refer the juvenile to services, or proceed with adjudication. This determination must be made within fourteen days after receipt of screening reports, unless good cause for extension is shown. The court may order further evaluation if initial results are inconclusive.

Before proceeding with a preliminary hearing, the court shall advise the respondent of the right to have the factual dispute determined by a judge rather than a referee. This advisement shall be made on the record. If the respondent does not waive this right in writing, the matter shall be assigned to a judge for determination of facts.

Upon forfeiture of bail in a delinquency proceeding, the court shall not enter judgment for the full amount unless the juvenile is brought before the court within thirty days after the date of forfeiture. If the juvenile is not produced within that period, the court may, on motion of the prosecuting attorney, order payment of the forfeited sum by the surety and any indemnitors, subject to applicable exemptions.

Upon entry of an order or judgment affecting a juvenile respondent’s substantial rights, the court shall provide the respondent with a written notice advising of the right to appeal and the procedure for obtaining appointed counsel on appeal. This notice must be served within seven days after entry of the order or judgment.

Before accepting a plea of guilty or no contest in a delinquency proceeding, the court must personally address the respondent under oath. The court shall inquire whether any person has promised any inducement other than that contained in the agreement or has threatened any penalty if the plea is not entered. The court must ensure the plea is voluntary and intelligent before accepting it.

If a juvenile has been detained for more than sixty days through no fault of the defense, the court shall release the juvenile without bond upon motion. This mandatory release applies unless the state demonstrates that detention is necessary to ensure appearance or protect public safety, and such justification must be supported by clear and convincing evidence presented within ten days of the motion.

Days during which a juvenile is detained pending disposition of a probation violation charge shall not count toward the twenty-four-hour commencement deadline for detention hearings, unless the court orders otherwise on motion showing good cause. This exclusion applies only to periods when the juvenile remains in custody solely due to the alleged violation.

Upon detention for probation violation, the probation officer shall refer the juvenile for mental health or substance abuse evaluation within twenty-four hours. The evaluator shall submit a written report to the court immediately upon completion. The court may consider this report in determining disposition. Failure to secure timely evaluation does not preclude detention if safety concerns exist.

The court shall inform the juvenile that they have the right to remain silent during any probation violation hearing. The juvenile’s refusal to speak or answer questions shall not be used against them in determining whether a violation occurred. This warning must be given prior to the commencement of the hearing, regardless of whether counsel is present.

Upon acceptance of a no-contest plea in a juvenile probation revocation proceeding, the court shall place on the record its rationale for accepting the plea. The court’s factual findings supporting the revocation must be based on evidence independent of the youth’s statements. This determination shall occur prior to entry of the order of revocation.

In delinquency proceedings regarding residential placement review, the rules of evidence need not be strictly applied. The court may admit any relevant information, including hearsay, if its probative value outweighs any prejudice. Parties must provide notice of evidence intended for admission. The court shall determine the weight and credibility of such evidence in deciding whether to modify or terminate the placement order.

A minor who escapes from state placement shall be detained without bond pending return to custody. The general bail framework does not apply. Upon capture, law enforcement must immediately notify the court and the placing agency. The court shall order detention unless the minor demonstrates that release poses no risk of further escape or danger to the community.

Upon filing a placement report, the court shall review the record and enter an order approving or rejecting the placement within fourteen days. If the court rejects the placement, it shall state on the record specific reasons for the rejection. Failure to act within fourteen days constitutes approval of the placement unless good cause is shown for an extension.

The court shall not transfer a juvenile to adult court based on findings from a preliminary examination if evidence admitted at that proceeding was obtained in violation of constitutional protections or rules of evidence. A party may move to suppress such evidence prior to the transfer hearing. The court must exclude inadmissible evidence when determining probable cause for waiver.

The court shall hold an initial appearance within forty-eight hours of detention, excluding weekends and holidays. If the time expires, the juvenile must be released immediately unless a petition for secure detention is filed and granted before expiration. Extensions require written findings that exigent circumstances prevented timely hearing and that continued detention serves compelling state interests.

Upon arrest on a juvenile warrant, the court shall conduct an initial appearance within forty-eight hours. This period excludes Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays. If the initial appearance is not held within this time limit, the court shall order the immediate release of the juvenile unless good cause for delay is shown.

A party may amend the charging document to include an adult-conviction bid at any time before the probable cause hearing without leave of court. The amendment must be filed and served on all parties within three days prior to the scheduled hearing. The court shall consider the amended allegations during the probable cause determination if properly filed and served in accordance with this rule.

The court shall hold a review hearing within thirty days before the juvenile’s nineteenth birthday. If the juvenile reaches age nineteen prior to the hearing, the court may continue the proceeding in juvenile court or transfer jurisdiction to adult court, provided notice is given to all parties at least ten days before the scheduled date.

Upon filing a petition in a child protective proceeding, the petitioner shall file a statement identifying all related pending cases involving the same parties. This statement must be filed with the court but need not be served on any other party unless the court orders otherwise. The statement shall be filed within ten days after the initial petition is filed or at such other time as the court directs.

Upon return of the minor to a legal custodian, the court may impose conditions necessary to ensure the child’s safety and well-being. Such conditions may include supervised visitation, participation in counseling or treatment programs, drug testing, or restrictions on contact with specific individuals. The court shall specify the duration and terms of each condition in the written order issued at the hearing.

If the petition involves an Indian child, the court shall comply with tribal placement preferences under federal law. Upon motion or sua sponte, the court must consult with the tribe to determine applicable priorities. Placement orders shall adhere to these preferences unless good cause exists. The court shall document compliance efforts in the record within ten days of the hearing.

On motion of a parent or guardian, the court may order the release of a child from protective custody upon posting a bond in an amount fixed by the court. The bond must be posted within three days after the hearing. Release is subject to the condition that the child’s safety and welfare will not be endangered and that the parent ensures the child’s appearance at all subsequent proceedings.

On motion of the Department or any party, the court may order a parent to disclose contact information for medical and dental providers treating the child within seven days. The order shall specify the scope of disclosure required for case planning purposes. Failure to comply may result in sanctions under Rule 2.312.

In removal proceedings involving an Indian child, the court shall require testimony from a qualified expert witness regarding the tribe’s parenting customs. The party seeking removal must prove by clear and convincing evidence that active efforts to prevent removal were made and that continued custody poses a serious detriment to the child, considering tribal cultural standards.

In child protective proceedings, the court shall require all parties to complete a standardized domestic violence screening instrument prior to mediation. Screening must be conducted individually and confidentially. If the instrument indicates a history of domestic abuse, mediation is prohibited unless the court finds, after an evidentiary hearing, that participation would not endanger any party or child.

A mediator assigned to child protection cases must complete foundational coursework in family dynamics, trauma-informed care, and Michigan child welfare statutes within one year of appointment. The court shall not assign a file to any individual who has not submitted proof of such completion. Failure to maintain current certification results in immediate removal from the roster.

Upon a plea of guilty or admission to a petition, the respondent waives the right to require the prosecution to prove each element of the offense beyond a reasonable doubt. The court may accept the plea based on the probation officer’s report and other available evidence without requiring witnesses to testify, provided the court determines the plea is made voluntarily and with understanding of its consequences.

On motion of the prosecution, the court shall hold a pretrial hearing to determine whether a child victim’s prior out-of-court statement possesses sufficient indicia of reliability. If the court finds the statement reliable and the victim is unavailable, the statement may be admitted as substantive evidence in the juvenile trial, provided the defendant had an opportunity to cross-examine the declarant or the circumstances surrounding the statement are adequately disclosed.

The Department shall present evidence demonstrating reasonable efforts to prevent or eliminate the need for removal. This proof must establish that services were offered to assist the family in maintaining a safe home environment. Failure to demonstrate such efforts constitutes grounds for denying continued custody, unless the court finds good cause for waiver based on immediate danger to the child.

Upon removal of a child from the home prior to adjudication, the court shall hold a protective custody review hearing within forty-eight hours of removal, excluding weekends and holidays. The court shall determine whether probable cause exists to believe the child is an abused or neglected child and whether continued placement outside the home is necessary for protection.

The court shall conduct periodic reviews of foster care placements pursuant to MCR 3.965. Evidence presented at such hearings is governed by the rules of evidence applicable in civil proceedings, except that hearsay may be admitted if its reliability appears reasonable. The court must consider all relevant information regarding the child’s safety, permanency, and well-being. Parties shall have the right to present testimony and cross-examine witnesses.

On motion of the Department of Human Services or a party, the court may permanently sever parental rights at an initial dispositional hearing if clear and convincing evidence establishes grounds under MCL 712A.19b. The motion must be filed within thirty days after adjudication. The court shall hold a separate hearing on the motion before entering an order of termination.

Upon determining indigency, the trial court shall appoint counsel for appeal. Within fourteen days of entry of the final order, the court must transmit a certified copy of the record to the appellate court and notify appointed counsel. Failure to transmit the record or provide notice within this period constitutes a waiver of any time limitation on filing a notice of appeal by indigent parties.

On motion to review an agency’s refusal to consent to guardianship, the movant shall file a petition stating grounds for relief. Within ten days after filing, the movant shall serve copies on the agency and any interested parties. The court may hold a hearing without further notice if good cause is shown. The agency shall respond within fourteen days.

On motion for contempt of a juvenile protection order in a court other than the issuing court, the caption must identify the original case number and issuing judge. Within five days after filing, the local clerk shall transmit copies of all pleadings to the clerk of the issuing court. The receiving court may proceed only upon confirmation that jurisdiction is proper under this rule.

The court shall conduct an initial appearance within forty-eight hours of detention, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays. If detention occurs on a Friday or immediately preceding a holiday, the appearance may be delayed until the next business day. The juvenile must be brought before the judge without unnecessary delay to determine probable cause and conditions of release.

If a parent or guardian is present, the court shall ask whether there is any reason to reject the admission. The court shall place the parent’s or guardian’s position on the record. This inquiry and recording requirement apply regardless of whether the child has entered an admission of guilt.

Upon adjudication of a juvenile for violating a personal protection order, the court shall conduct sentencing within 30 days. On motion of either party showing good cause, the court may extend this period for up to 60 days. Sentencing may not occur before the expiration of any applicable waiting period required by statute.

A party may move to alter or amend a judgment within 21 days after entry of the judgment. The motion must state the grounds therefor with particularity. If the motion is based on newly discovered evidence, it shall specify the evidence and why it was not presented at trial. The court may grant relief if justice so requires.

A party may appeal as of right from an order entered after adjudication in a child protective proceeding only if the order changes physical custody or legal status. An order that does not change physical custody is not immediately appealable as of right. Any other post-adjudication disposition shall be reviewed pursuant to MCR 3.965(C)(2) upon motion for leave to appeal.

Upon appointment of counsel in a child protective appeal, the lower tribunal’s signature on the order of appointment constitutes timely notice of entry for computing appellate deadlines. No separate filing or service of notice is required to commence the time period for filing a notice of appeal or other post-judgment motions.

Upon receipt of the draft order regarding a juvenile’s request for appellate counsel, the trial court must rule within fourteen days. If denying the request, the court shall issue an order specifying that the denial is based on a determination that the appeal lacks arguable merit or that the juvenile has not demonstrated indigency, and shall state the specific reasons for such findings.

These rules govern procedure in district and municipal courts. They apply to all civil actions, including small claims, unless otherwise provided by statute or these rules. Local court rules may supplement these provisions but shall not conflict with them. The trial courts shall administer justice efficiently, ensuring uniformity in practice while preserving the summary nature of proceedings in lower courts.

On motion of any party, the court shall transfer an action to circuit court if a cross-claim exceeds the district court’s jurisdictional monetary limit. The motion must be filed within twenty-one days after service of the pleading asserting the cross-claim. Upon transfer, the district court retains no further jurisdiction over the transferred claims.

The plaintiff shall state facts showing the defendant’s unlawful detainer and the plaintiff’s right to possession. The complaint must allege specific grounds for eviction, including lease violations or nonpayment of rent, sufficient to demonstrate that the tenant lacks legal justification to remain. Failure to include these essential allegations renders the pleading defective subject to motion for dismissal.

The defendant shall appear at the hearing time set forth in the summons to answer the complaint orally. Failure to appear constitutes a waiver of the right to present a defense. The court may proceed with judgment for possession upon plaintiff’s proof of service and entitlement, unless good cause is shown for continuance.

A tenant must file an answer within seven days after service of the complaint. The filing shall include proof of service upon the landlord’s attorney. If proof of service is not filed, the court may strike the answer or impose sanctions on motion by any party. Failure to respond within the prescribed time constitutes a default.

On motion by any party, the court may sever a monetary claim from a possession action if consolidation would unduly delay eviction proceedings. The court shall schedule a separate hearing for the severed claim within thirty days. Possession proceedings shall proceed independently unless the court orders otherwise to prevent manifest injustice.

On motion by a party asserting an equitable defense, the court shall determine whether the defense is substantial. If the court finds the defense substantial, it shall transfer the action to civil proceedings. The court retains jurisdiction until such transfer occurs. Failure to raise the defense within ten days after service of the complaint waives the right to equitable relief in summary proceedings.

On motion by the landlord demonstrating tenant’s failure to comply with rent escrow orders, the court shall schedule an immediate hearing. The hearing must occur within ten days of filing. By failing to maintain compliance, the tenant waives any right to a jury trial regarding possession. The court may summarily determine the matter based on the record and evidence presented at the hearing.

On the first day scheduled for the hearing, the court shall orally advise each litigant of their specific rights, including the right to counsel and the consequences of default. This advisement must occur before any substantive proceedings commence. Failure to provide this oral advisement does not invalidate the judgment but may constitute grounds for relief if prejudice is demonstrated. The court shall record on the docket that such advisement was made.

On motion of a party against whom a default judgment has been entered, the court may set aside the judgment for good cause shown. The motion must be accompanied by an affidavit or verified statement establishing that the moving party has a meritorious defense to the claim. The court shall grant relief only if the moving party demonstrates diligence in seeking to avoid the default and shows that setting aside the judgment will not prejudice the opposing party.

Upon finding the claim valid, the court shall enter judgment for forfeiture. The clerk must serve a copy of the order on the absent party within seven days by first-class mail. Service is complete upon mailing. The prevailing party may request proof of service from the clerk at any time.

A writ of garnishment may issue upon entry of judgment. If the judgment orders payment in installments, no writ shall issue until the expiration of the time for appeal or until a default occurs in any installment payment, whichever is earlier. The prevailing party must file a request for issuance with the clerk within 90 days after entry of judgment to preserve enforcement rights.

A defendant seeking to compel a formal complaint must file a motion within twenty-one days after removal. If no such motion is filed, the affidavit serves as the complaint for all purposes. The court may deny the motion if the affidavit provides sufficient notice of the claim. Failure to move waives the right to challenge the pleading's form.

A party may challenge a magistrate’s ruling by filing a motion within fourteen days after entry of the ruling. The motion must state specific grounds for the challenge. No filing fee is required for this motion. The district court judge shall review the record and rule on the motion. Failure to file a timely motion constitutes a waiver of the right to appeal the magistrate’s decision.

In an unopposed guardianship proceeding, the court may grant the petition without a hearing if the petition, supporting affidavits, and medical reports demonstrate clear and convincing evidence of incapacity or need for guardianship. If the court finds the record insufficient, it shall order a hearing where testimony must be presented to establish the necessary facts before entering an order.

Notice by publication shall be published once in a newspaper of general circulation within the county. Publication must occur at least fourteen days before the hearing date. If the hearing is scheduled less than fourteen days after the order to publish, notice may be given by other means approved by the court. The clerk shall file proof of publication with the court prior to the hearing.

If a party determines that a minor is a member of a federally recognized tribe after appointment, the party must immediately notify the court and serve notice on the tribe and parents. Upon such notice, the court shall vacate the prior order if required by federal law or tribal custom. The guardian’s authority remains valid only until the court enters a new order confirming compliance with applicable Indian Child Welfare Act requirements.

If another court has jurisdiction over the child, the probate court shall resolve the conflict under general rules for competing jurisdictions. A party filing a petition or motion must describe any earlier lawsuit involving the child. This description shall be included in the initial pleading or within ten days after learning of the prior proceeding, whichever is earlier.

A party filing a document in a probate proceeding must use SCAO-approved forms where available. Documents shall be signed by an attorney of record or the pro se party. The court may strike any document that fails to comply with these formatting and signing requirements. Compliance is mandatory upon filing, unless the court grants leave for good cause shown.

On motion, an attorney may appear limited to specific issues in a probate proceeding. The motion must specify the scope of representation and shall be filed within ten days after the attorney’s initial appearance. Unless the court orders otherwise, such limited appearance does not constitute general representation. Notice must be served on all interested persons.

On motion or the court’s own initiative, the court may permit amendment of pleadings at any time, including during trial or hearing, if justice so requires. Leave to amend shall be freely given when no undue prejudice results. The court may impose conditions, including service requirements, to prevent delay or prejudice to opposing parties.

A personal representative shall notify each beneficiary in writing of any pending litigation affecting the estate. The notice must advise that failure to file a motion to intervene within thirty days after service constitutes consent to be bound by the judgment. A beneficiary who does not timely move to join the action is deemed a party for purposes of res judicata and collateral estoppel regarding the subject matter of the litigation.

The guardian shall file an annual report with the court within thirty days of the anniversary of appointment. A copy must be served on the incapacitated person, if competent, and upon any spouse or adult children known to the guardian. Service may be waived by order of the court for good cause shown. Failure to timely file constitutes grounds for removal.

If the decedient is survived only by minor descendants, notice must be served upon the guardian of the estate or the personal representative appointed for such minors. If no guardian or representative has been appointed, notice shall be served upon the clerk of the probate court having jurisdiction over the minors’ residence, within ten days after filing the petition.

A proponent may file an affidavit of a witness to prove a will without notice. If an interested party objects within ten days after notice of filing, alleging lack of prior notice, the court shall require personal service of process on the objecting party before admitting the will to probate.

In contested probate proceedings, the Michigan Court Rules govern procedure unless this rule provides otherwise. A party seeking pretrial relief must file a motion stating specific grounds. The court shall decide the motion based on submissions and hearing. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in denial of the motion without prejudice.

In contested probate proceedings, the court may refer specific issues to settlement conference or neutral evaluation upon motion or sua sponte. The referral order shall specify the issues, the neutral’s qualifications, and the deadline for completion. Parties must participate in good faith. The neutral shall submit a written report within thirty days unless extended by the court.

A party requesting a jury trial in a probate proceeding must file a written demand. The demand shall be filed within ten days after service of the last pleading directed to the issue, or earlier if ordered by the court. A request embedded in another document without a separate filing is insufficient. Failure to timely file a proper demand constitutes a waiver of the right to trial by jury.

A party must submit a proposed order to the court within seven days after entry of judgment or order. The proposed order must be in writing, signed by the prevailing party’s attorney, and conform to the format prescribed by this rule. The court may modify the time for submission on motion for good cause shown. Failure to submit a proposed order within the specified time waives the right to propose specific language.

The clerk shall issue letters of authority only after the personal representative qualifies and files proof of surety coverage if required by the court. If a bond is ordered, issuance is conditioned upon filing satisfactory evidence that the surety has executed the bond or provided other security approved by the court. The clerk may not release fiduciary documents until all statutory and judicial requirements for qualification are fully satisfied.

On motion to suspend a personal representative’s authority or stay proceedings, the movant must serve notice on the personal representative and all interested persons at least fourteen days before the hearing. The court may grant relief only upon finding good cause. Failure to provide timely notice constitutes grounds for denying the motion.

Upon appointment of a temporary fiduciary, the powers of any previously appointed personal representative are suspended to the extent necessary for the temporary fiduciary to perform duties. The court may limit or expand these powers by order. No separate pleading is required to effectuate this suspension. The clerk shall notify all interested persons of the appointment and suspension within seven days.

The personal representative shall file an appraisal showing the property’s fair market value. If the court finds the appraisal does not reflect the probable sale price, it may order a new appraisal or require additional evidence before approving the sale. The court shall not approve the sale unless satisfied that the proposed price is reasonable and in the estate’s best interest.

If an interested party cannot be located for service of notice regarding the appointment of a personal representative, the court shall order publication in a newspaper of general circulation within the county. For purposes of this rule, "newspaper" means any periodical published at least once a week that contains news and public announcements. The publication must occur once, unless the court orders otherwise.

In an intestate proceeding, the petition must allege the decedent’s heirs at law and their relationship to the decedent. If no will is probated, the petitioner shall identify all persons entitled to share in the estate under the laws of descent and distribution. Failure to disclose beneficiaries at law constitutes grounds for dismissal or amendment of the petition.

The applicant shall publish notice of intent to apply for appointment in a newspaper of general circulation within the county. Publication must occur once, at least fourteen days before filing the application. If a person with equal priority cannot be located after diligent search, publication satisfies the notice requirement for that person. The affidavit of diligent search must accompany the application.

If no federal estate tax return was filed, the final account shall state that no state death duties are owed. The personal representative must file this statement with the final account within thirty days after the expiration of the period for filing a federal estate tax return, unless extended by order of the court.

On motion of the fiduciary, the court shall grant release from responsibility if the fiduciary files an account showing full administration of the estate. The court may grant the release without notice if no party objects within thirty days after filing. Otherwise, the court shall grant the release only after a hearing on proper notice to all interested parties.

Upon filing an objection to an emergency ex parte appointment of a temporary guardian, the court shall schedule a hearing within fourteen days. The court may extend this period for good cause shown. Notice of the hearing date must be served on all interested parties at least seven days prior to the hearing. Failure to schedule the hearing within the prescribed time does not invalidate the objection but requires immediate judicial action to resolve the dispute.

The court-appointed investigator shall conduct a reasonable inquiry into the child’s Native American heritage within thirty days of appointment. This inquiry must include contacting the child’s parents, legal custodians, and extended family members to determine if the child is an Indian child as defined by federal law. The investigator shall file a written report with the court detailing the findings of this inquiry.

Upon the death of a guardian for an adult with developmental disabilities, any interested person may petition the probate court for appointment as successor guardian. The petitioner shall file the petition within thirty days of notice of death. The court shall determine suitability based on the ward’s best interests and may deny appointment if evidence demonstrates conflict of interest or incapacity to serve.

On motion for approval of a settlement involving a protected person’s assets, the movant must file a verified statement detailing the terms and any compensation to fiduciaries. Notice shall be served on all interested parties at least fourteen days before the hearing. The court may approve the agreement only if it finds the terms are fair, reasonable, and in the best interests of the protected person, after considering the evidence presented.

Documents filed in involuntary treatment proceedings shall be open to public inspection unless sealed by court order pursuant to applicable law. A party seeking to seal documents must file a motion demonstrating good cause. The court shall rule on the motion within ten days. Absent a sealing order, all filings remain publicly accessible immediately upon filing.

On motion of an indigent party in a mental health proceeding, the court shall appoint a qualified physician for a clinical evaluation. The moving party may nominate a specific physician. The court must approve the nomination unless it finds good cause to deny it. If the court denies the nomination, it shall appoint another qualified physician within ten days.

Upon filing a petition for renewed commitment or discharge, the court shall issue notice to all persons who received notice of the original hospitalization proceedings. Notice must be served within fourteen days after filing. The court may extend this time for good cause shown. Failure to provide timely notice does not invalidate the order if actual notice was given.

In mental health proceedings, unless a statute expressly requires oral waiver in open court, a respondent may waive rights by executing a written instrument. The attorney of record shall witness the signature. The written waiver is effective upon filing with the clerk. The court may require personal appearance to confirm voluntariness on its own motion or that of any party.

A party challenging involuntary commitment without prior hearing must file a written motion within ten days of receiving notice. Upon filing, the court shall set the matter for an expedited hearing within five days. The court may extend these time periods only upon a showing of good cause. Failure to file timely results in waiver of the right to challenge the commitment order.

On motion filed within ten days of transfer, a party may demand a jury trial. The petitioner shall prove by clear and convincing evidence that the respondent poses a substantial risk of harm to self or others necessitating secure confinement. Failure to file timely waives the right. The court shall determine sufficiency of evidence if no jury is demanded.

On motion of the guardian, the court may authorize placement in a residential facility. The guardian shall file a petition detailing the proposed care plan and supporting evidence. Notice to interested parties must be given at least fourteen days before the hearing. The court shall approve the placement only if it finds the arrangement serves the ward’s best interests and complies with statutory requirements for developmental disability services.

In any proceeding concerning the release of a patient, the party opposing such release bears the burden of proving by clear and convincing evidence that the patient remains a danger to self or others or is gravely disabled. This burden applies regardless of whether the proceeding is initiated by motion or petition. The court shall determine release based on this evidentiary standard.

In proceedings involving termination of life-sustaining treatment or administration of involuntary psychotropic medication, the proponent shall bear the burden of proving by clear and convincing evidence that such action conforms to the patient’s known wishes or best interests. This heightened standard applies notwithstanding any general preponderance of evidence rule otherwise governing surrogate decision-making disputes.

On motion of any party, the court may stay proceedings pending appeal from an order appointing or removing a personal representative. Unless the court orders otherwise, the removal is effective immediately upon entry of the order. A stay does not automatically issue; the moving party must demonstrate irreparable harm and likelihood of success on the merits to obtain relief during the pendency of the appeal.

On motion of the prosecutor or probation officer, the court may issue a bench warrant if a probationer fails to report for three consecutive scheduled appointments or remains unreported for thirty days. Upon issuance, the probationer is deemed to have absconded from jurisdiction unless the court finds good cause for the failure to appear within fourteen days of the warrant’s entry.

On motion by a defendant detained for more than six months pending trial on a felony charge, the court shall release the defendant on personal recognizance unless the prosecution demonstrates probable cause to believe that release would pose a danger to the community or result in flight. The hearing must occur within ten days of the motion.

The court shall appoint separate counsel for each indigent codefendant unless the court finds no conflict of interest exists. Upon determining a potential conflict, the court must immediately assign independent representation to each defendant. A motion for separate counsel may be filed by any party or raised sua sponte by the court.

The trial court retains jurisdiction despite transfer defects unless objection is filed within fourteen days after notice of transfer. A party must object in writing to preserve the issue. Failure to timely object waives any challenge to the transfer’s validity, and the court shall proceed as if the transfer were proper. Jurisdiction vests upon filing of the complaint or information, regardless of clerical errors in the transfer documents.

If the arresting agency cannot arrange prompt transportation for an accused arrested outside the county where the offense occurred, the court may conduct the preliminary appearance by video conferencing. This procedure is permitted only if the defendant consents and the court finds that the use of technology will not prejudice the rights of the accused or impede the administration of justice.

On motion for pretrial release, the court shall consider the defendant’s ties to the community, including length of residence in the area and family relationships within the jurisdiction. These factors must be weighed against the risk of flight and danger to the community. The court may impose conditions reasonably necessary to assure appearance and public safety, provided such conditions do not violate constitutional rights.

Upon completion of the judicial review, the court shall certify the segregated portions of the grand jury materials. Within five days of certification, the clerk must distribute duplicate sets to both the prosecution and the defense. This distribution is subject to any protective order entered by the court regarding confidential information.

On motion of a party or sua sponte, after commencement of proceedings, the court may order separate trials of offenses joined in one charging document if it appears necessary to protect a defendant’s right to a fair trial or to avoid undue prejudice. Conversely, the court may join pending charges against the same accused for trial together if justice requires consolidation and no substantial prejudice results.

On motion by the prosecution, the court may hold an in camera hearing to justify a discovery shield. The hearing shall be conducted in chambers. The transcript of such proceedings must be sealed immediately upon conclusion. The sealed record is subject to review only on appeal, ensuring confidentiality of protected materials while preserving appellate rights regarding the shielding determination.

A party intending to introduce expert testimony or scientific evidence must serve written notice of such intent upon all other parties no later than fourteen days before trial. Failure to provide timely notice constitutes a waiver of the right to introduce such evidence at trial, unless the court, for good cause shown, grants leave to amend the disclosure.

A defendant entering a plea while reserving the right to appeal pretrial motions must file a written statement specifying the reserved issues within ten days of the plea entry. Failure to file such a statement constitutes a waiver of the right to withdraw the plea based on those issues. The court shall not accept the plea unless the reservation is explicitly recorded in the docket or filed with the clerk.

Before accepting a plea, the court shall advise the defendant that sentencing guidelines scores are provisional and may change upon completion of presentence investigation or other proceedings. The court shall inform the defendant that final sentencing determinations depend on accurate scoring calculations verified at a later date, ensuring the defendant understands potential variations in recommended sentencing ranges prior to entering a guilty or no contest plea.

If a plea is vacated, the prosecution may proceed on charges dismissed pursuant to the plea agreement only if those charges were not dismissed with prejudice. The court shall reinstate such charges upon motion by the prosecutor filed within fourteen days after entry of the order vacating the plea, unless good cause for delay is shown.

A party waives the right to trial by jury only if the waiver is in writing, signed by the party personally, and filed with the court. The court shall not accept a waiver unless it determines, on the record in open court, that the waiver is made knowingly, intelligently, and voluntarily after advising the party of the nature of the right being waived.

A criminal defendant may waive the right to a twelve-person jury by stipulating in writing to trial before fewer jurors. The court shall conduct an on-the-record colloquy with the defendant to ensure the waiver is knowing, intelligent, and voluntary. The stipulation must be filed prior to trial unless the court, for good cause shown, permits a later filing. The number of jurors shall not be less than six.

In criminal cases involving multiple defendants tried jointly, each defendant is entitled to ten peremptory challenges. The prosecution is entitled to fifteen peremptory challenges. If more than two defendants are tried jointly, the court may increase the number of challenges for each side, provided such increase does not exceed twenty per defendant and thirty for the prosecution. Challenges shall be exercised alternately, beginning with the defense.

On motion of a party or sua sponte, the court shall order redaction of victim contact information, including employer and religious affiliation, from the presentence investigation report before disclosure. The probation officer must comply within three days. Redaction is mandatory unless the court finds specific cause to retain such data for sentencing accuracy, in which case limited access protocols apply.

The probation officer shall deliver the presentence investigation report to the court and counsel at least seven days before sentencing. If the report is not delivered within that time, a party may move for continuance. The court shall grant the motion unless good cause exists to proceed without delay.

Before imposing sentence, the court shall afford each party an opportunity to confer with counsel regarding the presentence investigation report. This conference must occur within a reasonable time prior to sentencing, ensuring all parties have reviewed the report’s contents and recommendations. Failure to provide this opportunity constitutes grounds for remand or reconsideration of the sentence.

Upon granting an application for appointment of counsel, the trial court shall transmit to the administrative office of the courts a copy of the judgment, the order appointing counsel, and any motion for new trial filed by the defendant. If a motion for new trial is pending, the court shall transmit these documents within 14 days after entry of the order denying the motion or, if the motion is granted, within 14 days after entry of the new judgment.

An attorney appointed on appeal may appear at limited remand proceedings in the trial court if the appellate court determines such appearance is necessary to protect the interests of justice. The attorney shall notify the trial court and all parties within five days after the order remanding the case. Appearance is subject to the scope defined by the appellate court’s remand order.

A defendant seeking reinstatement of appellate rights shall file a motion within six months after final disposition of the post-conviction proceeding. A motion filed within three months is presumed timely. A motion filed after three months but within six months is presumed untimely unless the defendant demonstrates cause for the delay and actual prejudice resulting from the denial of appellate review.

The court may correct a sentencing order containing a clerical error or mathematical mistake on its own initiative within fourteen days after entry of the order. Before doing so, the court must provide written notice to all parties and afford them a reasonable opportunity to object. Any correction made under this rule does not alter the substantive rights of any party.

On motion of any party or sua sponte, the court may correct clerical errors in judgments or orders arising from oversight or omission. Such corrections must be made promptly upon discovery. A party seeking correction shall file a notice with the clerk and serve all parties within 14 days after entry of the judgment. The court shall issue an amended document reflecting the correction without prejudice to substantive rights.

Upon acknowledgment of a technical violation, the court shall continue probation and may modify conditions. The court may not revoke probation or impose incarceration solely for the technical violation. Modifications must be reasonable and related to rehabilitation. This determination is mandatory unless the defendant poses a danger to public safety.

The prosecutor need not file a reply to a defendant’s post-conviction motion unless the court orders one. If ordered, the prosecutor shall file the reply within twenty-one days after service of the order. Failure to file a reply when not ordered does not constitute waiver of any argument or defense. The court may extend these time limits for good cause shown.

The court may dismiss without response any claim lacking merit. For remaining claims, the court shall order the prosecutor to file a response within 21 days. The defendant may file a reply within 14 days after service of the prosecutor’s response. Failure to respond constitutes waiver of the claim.

Upon a party’s motion for appointment of counsel in a post-conviction proceeding, the court shall rule on the motion before scheduling any evidentiary hearing or requiring testimony. If the court denies the motion, it shall state its reasons on the record. No party shall be compelled to present testimony or evidence until the court has determined whether counsel must be appointed.

On motion for new trial, a defendant must demonstrate that the sentence imposed exceeds the maximum penalty offered in the rejected plea agreement. The court shall grant relief only if this disparity establishes prejudice resulting from ineffective assistance of counsel. The motion must be filed within twenty-one days after entry of judgment.

The court shall advise the defendant of rights and charges orally on the record or by providing written notice containing the required advisements. If written notice is used, the court shall place a copy in the case file and require the defendant’s signature acknowledging receipt. Failure to provide either oral or written advisement constitutes reversible error.

A defendant may move to withdraw a plea or set aside a judgment of conviction if the plea was not made voluntarily or was not supported by sufficient evidence. The motion must be filed within twenty-one days after entry of judgment. Failure to file within this period constitutes a waiver of the right to challenge the validity of the plea proceedings, except where required in the interest of justice.

An electronic citation filed as data is valid without a wet signature if the officer’s identity is electronically associated with the record. The filing party must ensure the system captures the officer’s unique identifier at the time of entry. No additional authentication is required unless the court orders otherwise on motion for cause shown.

The court shall retain jurisdiction over a juvenile placed on probation until age twenty-one if the juvenile was adjudicated delinquent for an offense that would constitute a felony if committed by an adult. This extended jurisdiction applies only upon the court’s written finding that continued supervision is necessary for public safety or the juvenile’s rehabilitation, and subject to periodic review every six months.

On motion for release, the court shall rule within five days. If the trial has not commenced and the court fails to rule within that period, the minor must be released immediately. This requirement applies regardless of whether the detention order was initially granted or modified.

If sentencing is not waived, the family division court shall determine disposition under MCL 712A.18b. The court may place the respondent on probation or declare them a ward of the state. This authority applies when the respondent is not sentenced as an adult. Orders must be entered within thirty days after adjudication, unless extended for good cause shown.

On motion for a minimum term of imprisonment, the moving party bears the burden of proving by clear and convincing evidence that the aggravating factors outweigh the mitigating factors. The court shall impose the minimum term only if it finds such preponderance. Failure to meet this burden requires imposition of the standard sentence range.

Before imposing a blended sentence, the court shall consider the juvenile’s prior participation in rehabilitation programs, including the nature of such participation and the results achieved. This factor must be weighed alongside other statutory criteria regarding the youth’s background to determine whether confinement or community supervision best serves the interests of justice and public safety.

The Department of Health and Human Services shall file a written status report with the court within thirty days after placement and every ninety days thereafter. The report must detail the minor’s current placement, progress toward case plan goals, and any changes in custody. Failure to file timely reports may result in sanctions or further judicial inquiry regarding the minor’s welfare and compliance with court orders.

These rules govern procedure in appeals from circuit court judgments. They do not extend or limit the jurisdiction of the Court of Appeals or the circuit courts. Compliance with these rules does not confer authority to hear an appeal where none exists, nor does it waive jurisdictional defects. The substantive power to adjudicate remains subject to statutory law and constitutional provisions.

A petition for review of an administrative agency decision shall be governed by these rules as if it were an appeal from a circuit court judgment, unless a statute or rule provides otherwise. The petitioner must file the petition within thirty days after the agency’s final order becomes effective. Service and filing requirements applicable to notices of appeal apply mutatis mutandis to petitions for review.

The circuit court may exercise jurisdiction over an agency ruling pending final determination if immediate review is necessary to prevent irreparable harm. A party must file a motion within ten days of the ruling. The court shall grant relief only upon a showing that direct appeal after finalization would be inadequate and that substantial prejudice will result from delay.

The applicant shall file a certificate stating whether the transcript has been ordered. If not ordered, the applicant must order it within fourteen days after filing the application. Upon ordering, the applicant shall file a certificate of ordering within seven days. Failure to comply may result in dismissal. The clerk shall notify all parties of the status of the record upon receipt of these certificates.

On motion of a party, the court may expedite consideration of an application for leave to appeal. The motion must state with particularity the reasons for the requested acceleration. The moving party shall serve the motion on all other parties and file it with the clerk. The court shall rule on the motion promptly.

A party filing a delayed application for leave to appeal shall attach an affidavit explaining the delay. Within fourteen days after service of the delayed application, any other party may file a response opposing the application. The court may grant or deny the application based on the affidavits and responses. Failure to file the required affidavit results in denial of the application.

The party posting the bond shall simultaneously lodge a certified copy with the trial judge. Within three days after service, the party must file proof of service with the clerk of court. Failure to file proof of service constitutes a waiver of the right to enforce the bond against non-parties. The court may impose sanctions for noncompliance.

If no party files a motion contesting the sufficiency of the security within fourteen days after filing, the stay of enforcement shall automatically terminate. Upon such expiration, the prevailing party may proceed to enforce the judgment without further court order. The clerk shall notify all parties when the stay expires and enforcement rights resume.

The appellant must order the complete record and file it with the circuit court clerk within thirty days after filing the notice of appeal. The appellant shall serve a copy of the transcript request on all other parties and file proof of service with the court. Failure to comply may result in dismissal of the appeal.

The appellant must procure the original transcript from the reporter. A party may reproduce the transcript for use in the appendix. Reproduced copies must be legible and conform to the original.
