If a dispute arises regarding the accuracy of a reproduction, the court may order the production of the original. The appellant shall serve copies on all parties within the time prescribed by these rules.

If the filing of a transcript is excused and a substitute record is filed, the clerk shall transmit the complete record to opposing counsel within ten days after the substitute is filed. This transmission requirement applies unless the court orders otherwise on motion for good cause shown. Failure to comply may result in dismissal of the appeal or other appropriate sanctions as determined by the circuit court.

The court shall issue its decision within 30 days after the hearing is concluded. If the court determines that good cause exists for a longer period, it may extend the time for issuing the decision. The extension must be noted in the record. A party may move for an expedited ruling if extraordinary circumstances warrant immediate action.

The appellant shall file the opening brief within 40 days after the lower court certifies that the record has been received by the appellate court. The time for filing may be extended by written stipulation of counsel not exceeding 30 days, or on motion and for good cause shown by the court.

On motion of any party, the court shall dismiss an appeal for abandonment if the appellant fails to file the brief within the prescribed time. A late-filed brief does not cure the default if filed after a notice of dismissal is served. The court may deny the motion only if good cause for the delay is shown before the hearing on the motion.

The Commission is not a party to the appeal. A petitioner must serve copies of all pleadings and notices upon the Commission and all interested parties within ten days after filing. Service upon the Commission does not confer party status or impose obligations beyond those expressly provided by statute or rule. The court shall treat the Commission as an administrative agency, not a litigant, for purposes of briefing schedules and judgment entry.

In appeals from civil service commission decisions, the appellant shall serve the head of the agency whose action is challenged at the Lansing office. The commission need not be made a party unless the court orders otherwise on motion for good cause shown. Service must occur within ten days after filing the notice of appeal.

A party seeking review of an administrative agency’s final order must file a notice of appeal in circuit court within 63 days after service of the order. If a timely request for rehearing is filed, the period for filing the notice of appeal runs from the date of service of the agency’s action on that request. Failure to file within this period deprives the court of jurisdiction.

The notice of appeal shall state the basis for the court’s jurisdiction and identify the specific order or decision being challenged. A party must file the notice within twenty-one days after entry of the judgment or order appealed from. Failure to include these particulars may result in dismissal. The clerk shall transmit a copy to the opposing party immediately upon filing.

In actions reviewing administrative agency decisions, this rule governs procedure not specifically addressed herein. General civil appellate rules apply to the extent they are consistent with this rule and do not conflict with statutory provisions governing judicial review of administrative action. Parties must comply with all applicable deadlines and filing requirements unless expressly modified by specific provisions for administrative appeals.

On motion to dissolve a stay of enforcement pending judicial review, the moving party shall serve notice on all other parties at least three days before the hearing date. The court shall give priority to motions affecting stays in administrative appeals over other matters on the docket, provided the motion is properly noticed and filed with the clerk.

When the Supreme Court assigns a visiting jurist to sit on an intermediate appellate court panel, no more than one visiting jurist shall serve on any three-judge panel. This limitation applies unless the Supreme Court expressly orders otherwise in writing for specific cases involving extraordinary circumstances or urgent public interest.

If an appellate court vacates a lower court’s final decision and remands the case, any subsequent order entered by the trial court that fully resolves all claims constitutes a new final judgment. A notice of appeal from this subsequent order must be filed within 21 days after entry of the order. This timeline applies regardless of whether the prior appeal was dismissed or decided on the merits.

If a party files a timely motion to reconsider or alter the judgment, the time for filing a notice of appeal runs from the entry of the order disposing of that motion. A notice of appeal filed before the disposition of such motion is ineffective and shall be treated as filed on the date the order disposing of the motion is entered.

If a timely motion for a new trial or to correct an illegal sentence is filed, any notice of appeal must be filed within fourteen days after entry of the order disposing of the last such pending motion. If no such motion is filed, the notice of appeal must be filed within twenty-one days after entry of judgment.

A party seeking to extend the time to appeal based on late service of the final order shall file an affidavit stating the date of receipt. The appellee may file a response disputing the facts stated in the affidavit within 14 days after service of the affidavit. If no response is filed, the facts are deemed admitted. The court shall determine the effective date of service based on the evidence presented.

The appellant shall file a docketing statement with the clerk of the Court of Appeals within fourteen days after filing the notice of appeal. The statement must affirm that the appeal was timely initiated and identify the basis for the appellate court’s jurisdiction. Failure to file the statement may result in dismissal of the appeal on motion of any party or on the court’s own initiative.

The appellant shall file a statement of facts limited to those necessary for decision. The court reporter’s transcript need not be filed with the notice of appeal. If the respondent disputes the statement, the respondent may file objections within ten days. The parties shall stipulate to the factual record or submit it to the trial court for determination before filing the record on appeal.

If a motion for reconsideration is filed within the initial period to appeal, the time to file an application for leave to appeal runs from the entry of the order disposing of the motion. A party must file the application within twenty-one days after the trial court enters the order ruling on the motion for reconsideration.

In an action challenging a redistricting scheme, the petitioner must file an affidavit from a qualified specialist attesting to the merits of the claim that the scheme is unlawful. This affidavit shall be filed concurrently with the petition or within seven days thereafter, unless the court grants leave for good cause shown. Failure to comply may result in dismissal of the action.

A party adversely affected by an order modifying or reversing a judgment may appeal to the supreme court. Any other party who was not a party to the original appeal and is adversely affected by such modification or reversal may, within 21 days after entry of the order, file a notice of cross-appeal. The cross-appeal shall be filed in the same manner as an initial appeal.

If the trial judge is unavailable, another judge of the same court may perform any duty required for the appeal. This includes signing orders, certifying records, or issuing mandates. The substitute judge shall act on motion or sua sponte to ensure timely processing. No delay in the appellate timeline results from this substitution.

Upon final disposition of an appeal resulting in affirmance or reversal with remand for sentencing, a defendant released on bond must surrender to the custody of the sheriff of the county where the trial court sits within ten days after entry of the mandate, unless the court orders otherwise. Failure to surrender constitutes contempt and may result in forfeiture of the bond.

A defendant released on bond pending appeal shall not change residence or employment without prior written approval of the Court of Appeals. On motion showing good cause, the court may grant leave to accept employment outside the state. Failure to obtain such approval constitutes a violation of bond conditions and may result in revocation of release.

On motion filed within fourteen days after entry of the order restricting access to briefs, a party may seek review of that restriction. The motion shall state specific grounds for relief. The court shall rule on the motion promptly. Failure to file a timely motion constitutes a waiver of any challenge to the restriction while the case remains pending before the appellate panel.

A party filing a document must serve a copy on every other party. Service shall be made by mail or electronic transmission. The filer must file a certificate of service with the document, stating the date and manner of service and identifying those served. Failure to file a certificate does not invalidate service if proof of actual delivery is shown.

A party filing a brief subject to a word limit must include a statement of the total number of words in the brief. This statement shall be placed at the end of the document, immediately following the signature block. The statement is part of the word count unless it appears on a separate page. Failure to include this statement constitutes noncompliance with the length requirements.

A pro se litigant relying on the special length allowance for typed appellate submissions must format the document in double-spaced type using a standard 12-point font. Margins shall be at least one inch on all sides. The text must not exceed the page limit prescribed for such submissions, excluding certificates of compliance and tables of contents. Failure to comply may result in rejection by the clerk.

The appellant shall state the facts relevant to the issues presented in chronological order. The statement must be complete and accurate, omitting no material fact unfavorable to the appellant’s position. Each factual assertion shall be supported by specific references to the record or transcript pages. Failure to comply may result in waiver of arguments relying on those facts.

A party seeking publication of an unpublished disposition must file a motion with the clerk within fourteen days after the disposition is issued. The motion shall state specific reasons why the disposition should be published. If no motion is filed within the prescribed time, the disposition remains unpublished and may not be cited as precedent.

On motion of any party or sua sponte, the court shall dismiss an appeal without oral argument if the parties file a stipulation for dismissal and all costs are paid. The clerk shall enter the order of dismissal immediately upon receipt of the stipulation and proof of payment, removing the case from the docket without further judicial action.

The court may schedule argument during recess only on motion demonstrating extraordinary circumstances requiring immediate resolution. A party must file the motion within fourteen days after briefing is complete. The moving party shall serve all adverse parties and file a certificate of service. The court shall grant leave to argue during recess only if delay would cause irreparable harm or significant prejudice to a party.

A party seeking review of an appellate court’s refusal to remand a case must include that assignment of error in the application for leave to appeal filed with the Supreme Court. Failure to raise the issue in the initial application constitutes a waiver of the right to challenge the refusal to remand on subsequent review.

On direct appeal by leave to the Supreme Court, the scope of review is limited to the grounds specified in the order granting leave. Absent an express expansion by the court, a party shall not raise arguments or issues not included in that order. The court may, on motion and for good cause shown, permit additional arguments, but such relief is discretionary and not guaranteed.

Upon final disposition, the clerk of the Supreme Court must transmit certified copies of the order to the lower court and the Court of Appeals. Within ten days after shipping the original case file, the clerk shall notify counsel of record by mail or electronic transmission. Notice is deemed complete upon mailing.

The appellee’s responsive brief must address arguments raised by the amicus curiae. The brief may also include affirmative arguments supporting the appellee’s position, provided such arguments were not previously presented in the initial brief. The court may grant leave to file additional responsive briefs on motion for good cause shown.

A party seeking to change the date of oral argument must file a motion stating good cause. If filed after the deadline for calendar agreement, the moving party shall pay a penalty. The court may deny the motion if the request is untimely and prejudices the opposing party or the administration of justice.

A motion for leave to file a late petition for rehearing is not permitted. Upon denial of an application for leave to appeal, any petition for rehearing must be filed within the time prescribed by these rules. No extension of time shall be granted, and the court lacks authority to accept untimely filings or motions seeking permission to submit them after the deadline has expired.

When the state court administrator convenes a gathering of judges, the presiding officer designated by the administrator shall conduct the meeting. The presiding officer must maintain order, facilitate discussion, and ensure compliance with established agenda items. All participating judges shall adhere to the directions of the presiding officer during the proceedings.

Upon entry of judgment, the clerk shall mail a copy to the prevailing party. If counsel failed to submit an extra copy with the proposed order, the clerk may charge a reasonable fee for preparation and mailing. Payment is due before delivery. Failure to pay does not delay entry but suspends mailing until receipt.

The clerk shall pay interest earned on deposited funds to the rightful owners, less a commission not exceeding two percent of the principal amount. This commission shall be paid into the State Treasury. Any remaining yield after deducting the capped commission must be distributed to the parties entitled to the underlying funds within thirty days of accrual.

Each trial court judge shall file a quarterly report with the chief judge detailing case dispositions and delays. This filing requirement applies regardless of whether the judge’s docket is clear or contains zero delayed cases. Reports must be submitted within thirty days following the end of each calendar quarter. Failure to file constitutes noncompliance with administrative duties, subject to disciplinary action by the state court administrator.

The court reporter shall record all oral proceedings, including testimony, arguments, and judicial rulings. Upon request by the court or a party, the reporter must transcribe specific spoken rulings into the official record within ten days. Failure to comply may result in sanctions. This requirement applies regardless of whether the ruling was entered on the docket separately.

The reporter shall retain custody of original recordings until the transcript is completed. Recordings may be removed from the courthouse solely for transcription purposes. Upon completion, the reporter must deliver the original recordings to the clerk within three days. The court may order immediate delivery on motion by a party or sua sponte if security concerns arise.

The board shall administer a proficiency examination for prospective court reporters twice each year. An applicant must achieve a passing score as established by the board to qualify for certification. The board may adjust the passing standard upon notice and comment, provided such adjustment does not conflict with statutory requirements governing court reporter qualifications.

If the chief judge is not assigned to the probate division, the judge assigned to that division who has served the longest shall perform the duties of the chief judge regarding probate matters. This designation remains in effect until a new chief judge is appointed or the current chief judge assumes those responsibilities.

The chief judge must oversee the court’s docket to ensure cases are resolved promptly. Within thirty days of assuming office, the chief judge shall establish procedures for tracking case disposition times. These procedures must require regular reporting on pending matters and identify causes of delay. The chief judge may adjust these procedures as necessary to maintain efficient administration of justice.

The chief judge shall assign cases to ensure equitable distribution. If a judge fails to comply with assignments or neglects duties, the chief judge may reassign pending matters. Persistent noncompliance constitutes grounds for disciplinary action under the Code of Judicial Conduct. The chief judge must report such conduct to the appropriate authority within 30 days of discovery.

The clerk of the court shall maintain custody of all original exhibits and settlement evaluation documents filed with the court. Upon request by a party or order of the judge, the clerk must produce such items for inspection or trial use. The clerk is responsible for the secure storage and inventory tracking of these case-processing materials until final disposition of the action or further order of the court.

The clerk shall maintain custody of the court file at all times. No portion of the file shall be removed from the clerk’s office without prior written authorization from the presiding judge. A party may request temporary access to specific documents on motion, subject to conditions imposed by the court to ensure preservation and security. Unauthorized removal is prohibited.

The clerk shall adopt a written policy governing access to records. This policy must include a schedule of fees for copying documents. The schedule shall specify the exact dollar amount charged per page for copies requested by litigants. The clerk must make this schedule available to the public upon request and post it on the court’s website within thirty days of adoption or any subsequent amendment.

The clerk shall provide copies of court-generated documents upon request. Before furnishing such copies, the clerk may require prepayment of the actual expenses incurred in producing them. Payment must be made within three days of demand. Failure to pay permits the clerk to withhold the documents until payment is received.

On motion of a client, the court shall order an attorney to refund fees if the attorney fails to provide a written fee agreement or itemized statement within fourteen days after demand. The court may award costs and reasonable attorney fees to the prevailing party. Service of the motion must include proof of prior written demand for refund.

A lawyer admitted pro hac vice for arbitration proceedings shall not appear in subsequent circuit court actions to vacate or confirm an award. To participate in such judicial proceedings, counsel must file a separate motion for admission pro hac vice. The court may grant the motion upon showing good cause and compliance with Rule 3.206(A).

The verified statement must attest that the attorney is familiar with Michigan law regarding Indian child custody proceedings and the rights of Indian tribes under federal and state law. The attorney shall certify this familiarity to ensure competent representation consistent with the purposes of the Michigan Indian Family Preservation Act. Failure to include this specific attestation renders the appearance ineffective.

The panel shall appoint one member with demonstrated expertise in domestic relations proceedings. This member must possess at least five years of experience interpreting in family law matters involving custody, support, or dissolution of marriage. The appointment shall be made within thirty days of the panel’s formation and subject to confirmation by the Administrative Office of the Courts.

The board shall recommend to the state court administrator standards for ongoing credentialing required to maintain interpreter certification. The state court administrator shall adopt such standards upon recommendation by the board, ensuring they meet minimum competency requirements established by rule. Adoption shall occur within 60 days of receipt of the board’s written recommendation.

Every interpreter must file an annual registration statement with the Commission by September thirty. Failure to file by that date requires payment of a late fee in addition to the standard registration fee. The Commission may deny registration if the statement is not filed within sixty days of the deadline, unless good cause for the delay is shown on motion and supported by affidavit.

The clerk of each third-class district court shall tally civil and criminal filings quarterly for cost allocation purposes. This tally must be completed within thirty days after the close of each calendar quarter. The clerk shall submit the final count to the State Court Administrative Office by the deadline established in the administrative office’s annual directive, subject to any adjustments required by statutory mandate or judicial order regarding fee distribution.

A bonded officer shall deposit all funds collected in an official capacity into a separate fiduciary account within three days of receipt. The officer must maintain these funds distinct from personal assets and disburse them only as ordered by the court or required by law. Failure to segregate such funds constitutes a breach of fiduciary duty and grounds for bond forfeiture.

For purposes of these rules, "attorney" includes any person admitted to practice law in this state, including those admitted pro hac vice or under temporary admission provisions. This definition applies regardless of current license status, provided the individual is authorized by court order to appear or assist in proceedings within this jurisdiction.

An attorney admitted to practice law in this state must comply with the Rules of Professional Conduct adopted by the Supreme Court. Admission constitutes a continuing obligation to maintain high standards of professional conduct and ethics. Failure to adhere to these standards subjects the attorney to disciplinary proceedings as provided by law. The Court retains exclusive authority to regulate attorney conduct and enforce compliance with ethical obligations throughout the period of licensure.

An attorney’s conviction of a felony or any crime involving moral turpitude, including violations of municipal ordinances, constitutes grounds for discipline. Upon such conviction, the attorney shall immediately notify the Attorney Grievance Commission in writing. Failure to provide timely notice may result in additional sanctions. The Commission may initiate proceedings based on the final judgment of conviction.

A suspension of an attorney’s license shall be for a definite period not less than thirty days. If the period exceeds one year, the suspension is indefinite until reinstatement is ordered by the Board or Court upon proof of rehabilitation and fitness to practice law. Indefinite suspensions require periodic review to determine if conditions for reinstatement have been met.

Mistakes or irregularities of procedure that do not affect substantial rights shall be disregarded. At any stage of the proceeding, the court may notice any error, defect, irregularity, or variance if it does not affect substantial rights and may order such relief as justice requires.

On motion of the administrator, the court may hold in contempt any respondent who fails to comply with a subpoena or order issued in a grievance proceeding. Upon such finding, the court shall suspend the respondent’s license to practice law until full compliance is achieved. The suspension remains in effect notwithstanding any pending appeal from the contempt order.

The respondent must serve a written reply within thirty days after service of the request for investigation. The reply shall be verified under oath or affirmation. Any false statement, misrepresentation, or concealment of material facts in the reply constitutes misconduct and may result in disciplinary sanctions, including suspension or disbarment, upon proof by clear and convincing evidence.

Each board member shall disclose any personal bias or prejudice regarding the respondent attorney within ten days of appointment. This duty to disclose is continuing throughout the proceeding. Failure to disclose such bias promptly may constitute grounds for recusal upon motion by a party, provided the moving party demonstrates actual prejudice resulting from the nondisclosure. The chairperson shall enforce compliance with this disclosure requirement.

If a respondent fails to comply with an order for pretrial fact-finding discovery, the grievance administrator may move for sanctions. Upon motion, the court shall impose appropriate penalties, including adverse inference or dismissal of defenses, if the failure causes unfairness or prejudice. The motion must be filed within ten days of the violation.

If the decision-maker rejects the second proposal or no revised agreement is submitted within twenty-one days of rejecting the first, the matter shall be referred to a hearing officer for trial. The hearing officer shall conduct proceedings and submit findings and recommendations to the court for final disposition in accordance with these rules.

Upon conclusion of proceedings, the adjudicator shall prepare a written report containing findings of fact, conclusions of law, and recommended sanctions. The adjudicator must file this report with the clerk within thirty days after the hearing concludes. The report constitutes the definitive record for judicial review unless modified by order of the court upon motion filed within fourteen days after service.

The Administrator shall serve a copy of the order to show cause on the respondent and the complainant at least 21 days before the hearing date. Service may be made personally or by first-class mail. If service is by mail, five additional days are added to the response period. The Board may shorten these time periods for good cause shown.

On motion by the grievance administrator alleging respondent’s incapacity, the hearing panel may order a physical or mental health evaluation if clear and convincing evidence demonstrates substantial risk of harm to clients or the public. The order shall specify the evaluator, scope, and timeline. Respondent must comply within fourteen days. Failure to submit to evaluation constitutes grounds for default judgment regarding incapacity.

A respondent asserting a medical or mental condition as mitigation shall bear the burden of proving such condition by clear and convincing evidence. Proof must be established through competent expert testimony submitted within thirty days after filing the answer, unless the court grants an extension for good cause shown. Failure to meet this burden precludes consideration of the condition in determining discipline.

A petitioner who has been charged with or testified in any criminal matter shall attach to the petition copies of all charging papers, judgments, sentencing orders, and records of disposition. These documents must be filed within thirty days after service of the notice of filing. Failure to provide such attachments constitutes grounds for denial of the petition without further hearing.

A fee arbitrator or practice monitor shall not be held liable for any act or omission performed in good faith within the scope of their official duties under the attorney discipline system. No civil action may be maintained against such an individual for conduct arising from the performance of these responsibilities, provided the act was not committed with malice or gross negligence. This immunity applies regardless of whether the conduct occurred before or after this rule takes effect.

Time served under an interim suspension shall be credited against any subsequent formal suspension imposed for the same misconduct. The court must calculate the final sanction period by deducting days of interim suspension from the total duration of the formal discipline. No credit is granted if the interim suspension was vacated or found invalid upon final review.

The State Bar shall reimburse out-of-pocket expenses incurred by members of grievance hearing panels and investigators. Reimbursement must be made within thirty days after the administrator approves the expense claim. Claims are subject to verification and compliance with applicable state travel and expense regulations. Failure to submit documentation within the prescribed period may result in denial of reimbursement.

The Commission and the courts shall interpret and apply these rules to ensure the integrity of the judiciary, protect the public interest, and maintain confidence in the administration of justice. In exercising their authority under this rule, they must prioritize the prompt and fair resolution of complaints while safeguarding the due process rights of judicial officers.

A complaint against a retired jurist must be filed within ninety days after the jurist’s retirement. The filing deadline is not tolled by the absence of prior complaints during service. If filed timely, the commission shall proceed with the investigation regardless of when the alleged misconduct occurred, provided the conduct falls within the jurisdictional scope of judicial discipline statutes.

The chief judge of each judicial circuit shall conduct the election of judicial discipline commission members within thirty days after the call for nominations. The State Bar of Michigan shall designate its representatives in accordance with its bylaws. All elections must be conducted by secret ballot, and results shall be certified to the Administrative Office of the Courts within ten days of the election date.

The Commission shall dismiss a complaint alleging judicial misconduct if the alleged conduct consists solely of an error in law or fact, including a mistaken ruling on the merits. A party’s dissatisfaction with the outcome of litigation does not constitute grounds for discipline. The Commission may investigate only when the complaint alleges conduct violating the Code of Judicial Conduct, independent of any legal error.

On motion of the disciplinary commission, the court may order a witness to testify remotely via video link during a pending grievance investigation. The order shall specify the technology platform and security protocols. The witness must appear at the designated time. Failure to comply constitutes contempt. This authority applies notwithstanding the absence of formal charges.

Before initiating formal proceedings, the commission shall notify the judge in writing of the allegations. The notice must specify that the judge may file a sworn response within thirty days. Failure to respond within this period constitutes a waiver of the right to contest the allegations at the preliminary stage. The commission shall consider any timely sworn response before determining whether probable cause exists to proceed.

Upon final conviction of a felony, the judge is automatically suspended without pay. The court shall hold the judge’s salary in escrow pending final disposition of the disciplinary proceeding. If reinstated, accumulated funds are paid; if removed, funds are forfeited to the state. This suspension occurs immediately upon certification of the conviction, requiring no further order from the judicial tenures commission.

The prosecutor must prove misconduct by clear and convincing evidence. The tenure commission shall conduct a formal hearing upon referral. Witnesses may be compelled to testify. The respondent has the right to confront witnesses and present evidence. Findings of fact and conclusions of law must be in writing. The commission shall issue its decision within 60 days after the hearing concludes, unless extended for good cause shown.

The Chief Justice may amend formal charges before final disposition. No reissuance of initial notice is required. If amended charges introduce new allegations, the respondent judge shall have fourteen days from service to file a written response. Failure to respond within this period constitutes a waiver of the right to contest those specific allegations. The Commission may extend this time for good cause shown.

The hearing officer shall file a written report containing findings of fact and conclusions of law with the Commission within thirty days after the close of evidence. The Commission may extend this time for good cause shown. The report constitutes the final decision unless the Commission orders otherwise or refers the matter to the Court.

On motion by the Commission, the chair shall schedule an evidentiary session to compel testimony. The Commission must serve written notice of the session on the judge at least fourteen days before the scheduled date. The notice shall specify the time, place, and subjects of inquiry. Failure to appear without good cause may result in sanctions or a finding of contempt.

Upon receipt of the commission’s report and recommendation, the Supreme Court shall review the record. The Court is not bound by the commission’s recommendation. It may adopt, modify, or reject the proposed discipline. The Court shall enter an order imposing appropriate sanctions, dismissing the complaint, or taking other action deemed necessary to preserve judicial integrity.

If the appointed lawyer is unable to serve, the State Bar of Michigan shall designate a substitute from its roster of qualified attorneys within ten days. The substitute must assume all duties of the original appointee immediately upon designation. Failure to designate a substitute within the prescribed period constitutes grounds for court intervention to ensure client protection and orderly administration of the suspended or incapacitated lawyer’s practice.

An interim manager reviewing client files shall maintain strict confidentiality regarding all privileged information. Mere assignment as interim manager does not constitute formal representation of clients unless expressly authorized by the court or agreed upon in writing with the client. The manager must act solely to preserve client interests and file integrity, without providing legal advice or initiating new litigation, until a successor attorney is appointed or the disability is resolved.

The court shall enter judgment within 28 days after receiving the clerk’s certificate of service of the opinion or order, unless the court orders otherwise on motion of a party for good cause shown. If no motion is filed, the clerk shall enter judgment immediately upon expiration of the period.

The clerk shall file the complaint with the court within three days after service of process is completed. If the party filing the complaint fails to serve process within one year after filing, the action shall be dismissed without prejudice on motion or on the court’s own initiative. This time period may be extended by the court for good cause shown upon application before the expiration of the initial period.

A party must serve a notice of appeal within 21 days after entry of the judgment or order appealed from. If a timely post-judgment motion is filed, the notice of appeal must be served within 21 days after entry of the order disposing of the last such pending motion. The clerk shall transmit the record to the appellate court upon receipt of the filing fee and proof of service.

The Michigan Court Rules govern procedure in all courts of record. They apply to civil, criminal, juvenile, and domestic relations proceedings unless a specific rule provides otherwise. The rules promote just, speedy, and inexpensive determination of every action. Courts shall interpret them to secure the ends of justice.

A party must serve and file a notice of appeal within 21 days after entry of the judgment or order appealed from, unless another time is prescribed by law. If a timely motion under MCR 2.610, 2.611, or 2.612 is filed, the time for appeal runs from entry of the order disposing of the last such motion.

A party must serve a copy of the summons and complaint on each defendant within 14 days after filing the complaint. Service may be made by any person who is not a party and is at least 18 years of age. Proof of service must be filed with the court within 21 days after filing the complaint, unless good cause for extension is shown.

On motion of any party or on its own initiative, the court may order that discovery be conducted in a sequence different from that prescribed by this rule. The court shall specify the sequence and timing of discovery activities to avoid undue delay, expense, or prejudice. The order may limit the scope, method, or duration of discovery for specific parties or subjects.

The court shall enter judgment within 28 days after receipt of the opinion or order, unless the court orders otherwise. If the opinion or order does not dispose of all claims and parties, the court may direct entry of judgment on specific claims or parties. A party may move for entry of judgment if the court fails to do so within that time.

A party may move to amend a pleading at any time with leave of court. Leave shall be freely given when justice so requires. If no answer has been filed, a party may amend once as a matter of course within 21 days after serving the pleading. The court may impose conditions on granting leave to protect against prejudice.

On motion of any party, the court may order discovery to be conducted in a different sequence or manner than prescribed by these rules if it determines that such modification is necessary for good cause shown. The court shall specify the terms and conditions of any such order, including deadlines for completion, to ensure fairness and efficiency in the proceedings.

On motion of any party, the court may order discovery to be conducted in a sequence different from that specified in this rule. The order must specify the sequence and timing of discovery activities. The court shall consider the convenience of witnesses and parties, the need for expedition, and the interests of justice when issuing such an order.

A party must serve a written notice of appeal within 21 days after entry of the judgment or order appealed from, unless a different time is prescribed by law. The notice must be filed with the clerk of the trial court and served on all parties to the action. Failure to file within the prescribed time may result in waiver of the right to appeal.

A party must serve a statement of issues within 28 days after filing a notice of appeal. The statement must concisely state each issue presented for review, with brief references to the record. Failure to file the statement constitutes a waiver of all issues not stated. The court may extend the time on motion showing good cause.

On motion of any party, the court may order that discovery be conducted in such sequence or manner as is just, including limiting the scope of discovery to prevent undue burden or expense. The court shall consider the needs of all parties and the interests of justice when determining the timing and extent of discovery proceedings.

On motion of a party, the court may order discovery to be conducted in a sequence different from that prescribed by this rule. The court shall specify the sequence and timing of discovery acts. This authority applies when necessary to prevent undue delay, hardship, or expense, or to ensure fair administration of justice.

A party must file a notice of appeal within twenty-one days after entry of judgment or order appealed from. If a party files a timely post-judgment motion under MCR 2.6, the time to appeal runs from entry of the order disposing of that motion. The clerk shall transmit the record to the appellate court upon receipt of the filing fee and proof of service.

A party must serve a notice of appeal within 21 days after entry of the judgment or order appealed from. If a timely post-judgment motion is filed, the notice of appeal must be served within 21 days after entry of the order disposing of the last such motion. The clerk shall transmit the record to the appellate court upon request.

The court shall set a case for trial within 182 days after the filing of the complaint or the filing of any responsive pleading, whichever is later. The court may extend this period on motion showing good cause. Failure to comply with this rule does not affect the validity of subsequent proceedings.

The court shall enter judgment within 28 days after receipt of the magistrate’s findings and recommendations. A party may file objections to the findings and recommendations within 14 days after they are served. If no objections are filed, the court may adopt the findings and recommendations without further review.

A party must file a notice of appeal within 21 days after entry of the judgment or order appealed from. If a timely postjudgment motion is filed, the notice of appeal must be filed within 21 days after entry of the order disposing of the last such pending motion. The clerk shall transmit the record to the appellate court upon receipt of the filing fee and proof of service.

On motion of any party or on its own initiative, the court may order that discovery be conducted in stages or by alternative methods. The court shall consider whether such an order will promote the just, efficient, and economical determination of the action. Any such order must specify the scope, timing, and manner of the discovery process to ensure fairness and prevent undue burden on any party.

On motion of any party or on its own initiative, the court may order an amendment to a judgment or order to correct a clerical error or to reflect a decision already made by the court. Such amendments must be made within a reasonable time after discovery of the error, without notice to other parties, unless the court orders otherwise.

On motion of any party, the court may order that discovery be conducted in a sequence different from that prescribed by this rule. The court shall specify the sequence and timing of such discovery. A party seeking an order under this subdivision must show good cause for deviation from the standard procedures.

A party may move to amend or supplement an answer or other responsive pleading at any time before trial, with leave of court if necessary. The court shall freely give leave when justice so requires. A party need not obtain leave to amend once within 21 days after serving the pleading, unless the opposing party has already filed a response.

The court shall set a case for trial within one year after the filing of the complaint. If the case is not set for trial within that time, any party may move to dismiss the action without prejudice. The court may extend the time for good cause shown. Failure to object to the delay waives the right to dismissal under this rule.

The court shall enter judgment within 28 days after receiving the findings and conclusions. If the court does not enter judgment within that time, a party may move for entry of judgment. The motion must be served on all parties and filed with the clerk. The court shall rule on the motion promptly.

A party must file a notice of appeal within 21 days after entry of the judgment or order appealed from. If a timely post-judgment motion is filed, the time to appeal runs from entry of the order disposing of the last such motion. The clerk shall transmit the record to the appellate court upon receipt of the filing fee and proof of service.

Within 21 days after service of the complaint, a defendant shall serve an answer or motion under rule 2.110(C) on each other party and file it with the court. Service of a motion permitted under this subrule extends the time to answer until 7 days after notice that the motion is denied or, if granted, until 7 days after service of the amended pleading.

A party seeking to amend an answer must file the amendment within 21 days after service of the pleading containing the claim or defense sought to be amended, or within 21 days after service of a motion under MCR 2.116(C) or (F), whichever is later. The court may grant leave to amend on just terms.

A party may move for summary disposition of all or part of an action. The motion shall be served at least 21 days before the time fixed for hearing. Opposing parties may serve responses within 14 days after service of the motion. Replies may be served within 7 days after service of a response. The court shall grant the motion if pleadings, depositions, answers to interrogatories, admissions, and affidavits show no genuine issue of material fact.

The court shall enter judgment within 28 days after receipt of the clerk’s certificate of compliance or notice of noncompliance. If the clerk does not certify compliance, the court may extend the time for entry of judgment on motion and for good cause shown. Failure to file a post-judgment motion within the prescribed time constitutes a waiver of objections to the judgment.

The court shall file its findings of fact and conclusions of law within 28 days after receiving the final post-trial brief or the expiration of the time for filing such a brief, whichever is earlier. If the court fails to file them within that period, any party may move for entry of judgment based on the evidence presented at trial.

Within 28 days after service of the complaint, a defendant shall serve an answer or a motion under Rule 2.110(C). If a party has requested a stay of proceedings under Rule 2.306(A), the time to respond is extended until 28 days after the stay is lifted. Failure to respond within this period may result in default judgment.

On motion of a party, the court may order discovery to be conducted in a different sequence or manner than specified in this rule if it determines that such modification is necessary for the just, efficient, and inexpensive determination of the action. The court shall consider the convenience of the parties and witnesses, the burden on the parties, and the need for prompt resolution.

A party must serve and file a notice of appeal within 21 days after entry of the judgment or order appealed from, unless a different time is prescribed by law. If a timely motion affecting the judgment or order is filed, the notice of appeal must be served and filed within 21 days after entry of the order disposing of the last such motion.

A party seeking to amend a pleading must file a motion with the court. The motion shall state the grounds for amendment and the proposed changes. If the opposing party does not object within 14 days after service of the motion, the court may grant the amendment without further hearing. Failure to respond constitutes consent to the requested relief.

On motion of any party, the court may order an amendment to a judgment or order to correct a clerical error arising from oversight or omission. The motion must be filed within 28 days after entry of the judgment or order. The court may act on its own initiative within the same period.

On motion of a party, the court may order that discovery be conducted in stages or by specific methods. The court shall specify the time limits for completing each stage or method. Discovery shall not exceed the scope permitted by this rule unless the court orders otherwise for good cause shown. Parties must comply with any such order regarding the sequence and manner of discovery.

A party must serve a notice of intent to appeal within 21 days after entry of the judgment or order sought to be reviewed, unless a different time is prescribed by law or court rule. Failure to timely file such notice constitutes a waiver of the right to appeal, except as otherwise provided in these rules or by statute governing specific proceedings.

A party must file a notice of appeal within 21 days after entry of the judgment or order appealed from. If a timely motion is filed under MCR 2.612, the time to appeal runs from entry of the order disposing of the final postjudgment motion. The clerk shall transmit the record to the appellate court upon receipt of the filing fee.

The court shall hold a hearing on the motion for summary disposition if any party files a statement of material facts not in dispute, or objects to such statements, within 21 days after service of the motion. If no objection is filed, the court may grant the motion without a hearing.

The court shall order discovery to proceed in phases if it determines that such an order will promote the fair and expeditious resolution of the case. The court may limit the scope of discovery, including the number of depositions or interrogatories, to prevent undue burden or expense. Parties must comply with any phased discovery schedule established by the court.

The court shall grant leave to file an amended pleading if justice so requires. A party seeking amendment must file a motion specifying the proposed changes. The opposing party may respond within 14 days after service of the motion. The court may deny leave if the amendment is frivolous, causes undue delay, or prejudices the adverse party’s substantial rights.

On motion of any party, the court may order that discovery be conducted in a sequence different from that prescribed by this rule. The court shall specify the sequence and timing for each type of discovery procedure. The order may limit the number of depositions or interrogatories, require notice before discovery, or provide for protective orders as necessary to prevent undue burden or expense.

On motion of a party, the court may order discovery to be conducted in a sequence other than that specified in this rule. The court shall specify the sequence and timing of discovery activities. The order must state the reasons for deviating from the standard sequence. Discovery shall proceed according to the court’s order unless modified by subsequent stipulation or further court order.

A party seeking to amend a judgment or order must file a motion within 21 days after entry of the judgment or order. The court may grant leave to file the motion after the 21-day period if good cause is shown. The motion shall state with particularity the grounds for relief sought and specify the amendment requested.

On motion of any party, the court shall order discovery to be stayed or limited if the court finds that the burden or expense of the proposed discovery outweighs its likely benefit, considering the needs of the case, the amount in controversy, the parties’ resources, the importance of the issues at stake, and the importance of the discovery in resolving the issues.

On motion of a party for good cause shown, the court may permit amendment or supplementation of the jury instructions after submission to the jury. The court shall state its reasons on the record. Any such amendment must be made within a reasonable time before the jury retires to deliberate, unless the interests of justice require otherwise.

The court shall hold a pretrial conference within 30 days after the filing of the answer or a motion to dismiss, whichever is later. The parties must attend with counsel authorized to settle. The court may issue orders regarding discovery, motions, and trial preparation. Failure to appear without good cause may result in sanctions.

A party seeking to appeal from an order granting or denying a motion for new trial shall file a notice of appeal within 21 days after entry of the order. If no such motion is filed, the time for filing a notice of appeal runs from entry of judgment. The court may extend the time for good cause shown.

On motion of any party, the court shall order the parties to submit a joint statement of uncontested facts and a brief statement of disputed issues. The statement shall be filed within 14 days after entry of the order. Failure to file may result in dismissal or default judgment.

A party seeking to amend a judgment or order must file a motion within 28 days after entry of the judgment or order. The motion shall state with particularity the grounds for relief. If the motion is based on newly discovered evidence, the movant must show that the evidence could not have been discovered earlier through due diligence and that it would likely change the outcome.

The court shall order the parties to meet and confer regarding discovery disputes. Within 14 days after filing a motion for discovery relief, the moving party must file a statement certifying that this conference occurred. The statement shall identify the issues discussed and any agreements reached. Failure to comply may result in sanctions or denial of the motion.

A party seeking to appeal from a judgment or order must file a notice of appeal within 21 days after entry of the judgment or order sought to be reviewed. If a timely motion under MCR 2.612 is filed, the time for filing a notice of appeal runs from the entry of the order disposing of the last such pending motion.

A party seeking to appeal from a judgment or order must file a notice of appeal with the clerk of the trial court within 21 days after entry of the judgment or order sought to be reviewed. Failure to file a timely notice of appeal constitutes a waiver of the right to appellate review, except as otherwise provided by law or court rule.

On motion of any party, the court may order that discovery be conducted in such sequence or manner as is just. The court may limit the number of depositions or interrogatories, shorten time periods for responses, and require disclosure before discovery. Such orders shall be made to avoid undue delay, expense, or prejudice to any party.

The court shall hold a hearing on the motion for postconviction relief if the respondent fails to file a response within 21 days after service of the motion, unless the respondent files a motion for extension of time and shows good cause for the failure to respond. The court may grant or deny the motion based on the pleadings and record.

The court shall set a date for trial within 120 days after the filing of a notice of removal or the filing of an answer, whichever is later. The trial date may be extended only upon a showing of good cause and by order of the court. Failure to comply with this rule does not affect the validity of any judgment entered.

A party seeking to appeal from a judgment or order must file a notice of appeal with the trial court clerk within 21 days after entry of the judgment or order. If a timely motion under MCR 2.612 is filed, the time for filing the notice of appeal runs from the entry of the order disposing of the last such motion.

On motion of a party, the court may order discovery to be stayed or limited if the moving party shows that the requested discovery is unduly burdensome, oppressive, or duplicative. The court shall specify the scope and timing of any permitted discovery. A party must comply with the court’s order within the time prescribed by the court.

A party seeking to appeal from a judgment or order must file a notice of appeal with the trial court clerk within 21 days after entry of the judgment or order sought to be reviewed. Failure to file a timely notice of appeal constitutes a waiver of the right to appellate review, unless good cause is shown for the delay.

The court shall schedule a status conference within 30 days after filing of the complaint. The parties must appear at the conference. On motion of any party, the court may modify the scheduling order for good cause shown. Failure to appear constitutes consent to default judgment.

On motion of any party, the court may order discovery to be conducted in a manner different from that prescribed by these rules. The order shall specify the scope, timing, and method of discovery. Such modification is permitted when necessary to prevent undue delay, expense, or prejudice, or to accommodate unique circumstances surrounding the case.

The court shall enter an order of protection if the petitioner demonstrates that respondent has committed domestic violence or stalking. The order may include provisions restraining respondent from contacting, harassing, or threatening petitioner. The court shall specify the duration and terms of relief necessary to protect petitioner’s safety and well-being, consistent with statutory requirements for emergency protective orders.

Upon filing of a notice of appeal, the clerk shall promptly transmit to the appellate court a copy of the judgment or order appealed from and any other documents required by law. The transmission shall occur within seven days after the notice is filed, unless the court orders otherwise for good cause shown.

The clerk of court shall file with the circuit court clerk a certified copy of the judgment or order within 14 days after entry, unless good cause is shown for additional time. The filing must include any notice of appeal required by law. Failure to file within the prescribed period does not affect the validity of the judgment but may subject the clerk to disciplinary action.

If the court finds that good cause exists for extending the time to file a notice of appeal, the court may extend the time for not more than 30 days after the expiration of the original period. An extension under this subdivision may be granted on motion filed before or after the expiration of the original period.

The court shall set aside a default judgment if the moving party shows good cause for the failure to respond. A motion to set aside must be filed within 21 days after entry of the judgment, unless the court orders otherwise. The court may impose conditions it deems just, including payment of costs or filing of a responsive pleading.

The court shall grant leave to file an amended complaint if justice so requires. A motion for leave to amend must be filed within 21 days after service of a pleading that raises a defense or counterclaim, or within 21 days after entry of an order dismissing the action, whichever is later. The moving party must serve the motion on all other parties.

On motion of a party, the court may extend the time for filing a notice of appeal if good cause is shown. The motion must be filed within 30 days after the expiration of the time prescribed by MCR 7.205(A). The court shall grant the extension only if the moving party demonstrates that failure to file timely was not due to lack of diligence.

On motion of any party, the court shall order the parties to submit a joint statement of uncontested facts and a separate statement of disputed issues. The statements must be filed within 21 days after entry of the order for summary disposition. Failure to file constitutes an admission that the opposing party’s statements are true.

If the court finds that the defendant is indigent, it shall appoint counsel. The court must order the attorney to file a notice of appearance within 14 days after appointment. Failure to file the notice constitutes grounds for discharge of counsel and appointment of new counsel, unless good cause is shown for the delay.

Within 21 days after entry of judgment, a party may file a motion for new trial or to alter or amend the judgment. The motion must state the specific grounds therefor. If the motion is based on matters occurring after the trial, the movant shall attach affidavits or other evidence supporting those grounds. The court may grant relief if justice requires it.

On motion of any party, the court may order discovery to be conducted in a manner that protects trade secrets or other confidential research, development, or commercial information. The order shall specify the conditions under which discovery is permitted, including limitations on access and use, and may require parties to file documents under seal.

The court shall grant a continuance if good cause is shown. Good cause includes the unavailability of essential witnesses or evidence, provided the moving party exercised due diligence to secure their presence. The motion must be filed promptly upon discovery of the need for continuance and served on all parties.

The court shall order the parties to file a joint statement of facts not in dispute. The statement must be filed within 14 days after the conference or on such other date as the court may direct. Failure to file the statement constitutes a waiver of any objection to the omission of facts from the statement.

On motion of a party, the court may order discovery to be conducted in phases or limit the scope of discovery to particular issues. The court shall consider whether the proposed limitation serves to avoid unnecessary expense or delay and promotes the just determination of the action. Any such order must specify the subjects, methods, and time limits for the permitted discovery.

Unless otherwise ordered by the court, a party must file a notice of appeal within 21 days after entry of the judgment or order appealed from. If a timely post-judgment motion is filed under MCR 2.610(C), the time to appeal runs from entry of the order disposing of that motion. The clerk shall transmit the record on appeal upon receipt of the required filing fees and proof of service.

A party must file a notice of appeal within 21 days after entry of the judgment or order appealed from. If a timely postjudgment motion is filed under MCR 2.610, the time to appeal runs from the entry of the order disposing of the last such motion. The clerk shall serve copies on all parties. Failure to file within this period bars appellate review unless good cause is shown.

A party shall file a notice of appeal within 21 days after entry of the judgment or order appealed from. If a motion specified in MCR 7.2(A) is filed, the time to appeal runs from entry of the order disposing of the last such remaining motion. The clerk shall transmit the record to the appellate court upon receipt of the filing fee and proof of service.

The court shall appoint counsel for an indigent defendant within 14 days after arraignment if the defendant requests representation and demonstrates financial inability to employ counsel. The appointment order must specify the scope of representation and notify the defendant of the right to consult with appointed counsel before any further proceedings.

A party must file a notice of appeal within 21 days after entry of the judgment or order appealed from, unless a different time is prescribed by law. The notice must be filed with the clerk of the trial court and served on all parties to the action. Failure to file within the prescribed time constitutes a waiver of the right to appeal.

A party seeking to amend a judgment or order must file a motion within 28 days after entry of the judgment or order. The court may grant leave to file the motion after the 28-day period has expired if good cause is shown. A copy of the motion shall be served on all parties.

If the court orders discovery, it shall specify the time for completing discovery. The court may extend or shorten the time for discovery upon motion and for good cause shown. A party must serve its discovery requests within the time specified by the court order. Failure to comply with a discovery order may result in sanctions as provided by law.

On motion of a party or on its own initiative, the court may order an evidentiary hearing to determine whether a defendant is competent to stand trial. The hearing shall be held within 30 days after the motion is filed unless good cause is shown for a continuance. The moving party must serve notice on all other parties at least 14 days before the hearing date.

A party must serve a notice of appeal within 21 days after entry of the judgment or order appealed from. The clerk shall transmit the record to the appellate court within 30 days after receipt of the notice. A party may move for extension of time to file the notice, but the motion must be filed before the expiration of the original period.

The court shall appoint counsel for an indigent defendant within 14 days after arraignment if the defendant requests representation and demonstrates financial inability to retain counsel. If no request is made, the court may appoint counsel at any time before trial if it determines that justice requires such appointment.

A party seeking to file an amended complaint shall serve it on all other parties within 14 days after entry of judgment, unless the court orders otherwise. Service may be made by first-class mail or personal delivery. If served by mail, three additional days are added to any period computed from the date of service. The clerk shall note the filing on the docket upon receipt.

The court shall set a date for sentencing within 180 days after entry of judgment or plea of guilty. If sentencing is not completed within that period, the court may extend the time for good cause shown on the record. Failure to sentence within the prescribed time does not affect the validity of the judgment or sentence.

A party seeking to appeal from a judgment or order must file a notice of appeal with the trial court clerk within 21 days after entry of the judgment or order sought to be reviewed, unless a different time is prescribed by law. Failure to file a timely notice of appeal deprives the appellate court of jurisdiction to hear the appeal.

The court shall issue its decision within 21 days after the last brief is filed or the oral argument concludes, whichever is later. If the court fails to issue a decision within that time, any party may move for expedited consideration. The court may extend the time for good cause shown.

The court shall set a case for trial within 18 months after filing or within 6 months after joinder of all parties, whichever is later. A party may move for additional time to prepare for trial. The court may grant the motion if it finds good cause. Failure to set a case for trial does not waive any defense or objection.

On motion of a party, the court may order discovery to be conducted in phases or limit the scope of discovery to particular issues. The court shall consider whether the proposed limitation promotes efficiency and avoids undue burden or expense. Any such order must specify the time limits for completing each phase and identify the specific issues subject to the limitation.

The court shall appoint an attorney for an indigent defendant if the defendant is charged with a crime punishable by imprisonment. The appointment shall be made at the earliest practicable time, but no later than the initial appearance. If the defendant requests counsel and appears without an attorney, the court shall inquire into the defendant’s financial status to determine eligibility for appointed counsel under this rule.

Within 14 days after entry of judgment, a party intending to appeal must file with the clerk a notice of appeal specifying the party or parties taking the appeal and the judgment, order, or part thereof appealed from. The notice shall be filed in the court that rendered the judgment. Failure to file a timely notice of appeal deprives the appellate court of jurisdiction.

If the defendant is represented by counsel, the court shall appoint counsel for any indigent defendant who requests representation. The court must determine indigency based on the defendant’s financial resources. Appointment shall occur before trial or at such other time as justice requires. Counsel appointed under this rule shall provide effective assistance throughout all stages of the proceedings.

On motion of any party, the court may order that discovery be conducted in phases or that specific matters be reserved for later discovery. The court shall specify the scope and timing of such phased discovery. This authority applies to limit discovery burden when appropriate, ensuring efficient case management while preserving parties' rights to obtain relevant evidence necessary for fair adjudication of claims.

On motion of a party, the court may order that discovery be conducted in stages or by alternative methods if the court finds that such measures are necessary to protect a party from undue burden, expense, or prejudice. The court shall specify the scope and timing of any ordered discovery.

The court shall schedule a hearing on the motion within 14 days after filing. If the motion involves a claim of ineffective assistance of counsel, the court may appoint counsel for the movant if the movant is indigent and lacks representation. The court shall issue an order granting or denying the motion within 30 days after the hearing.

The court shall order discovery to be completed within the time specified in the scheduling order. If no scheduling order has been entered, discovery must be completed within 120 days after the first defendant answers or moves under MCR 2.110(C). The court may extend this time for good cause shown.

On motion of any party or on its own initiative, the court may order a new trial for any reason that would justify one under common law. The motion shall be filed within 28 days after entry of judgment. If supported by affidavits, opposing affidavits may be filed within 14 days after service. The court may require oral argument.

On motion of a party, the court shall order discovery to be completed within a specified time. The order must state the date by which discovery shall be completed and may include other provisions necessary to ensure that discovery proceeds in an orderly manner. Failure to comply with the order constitutes good cause for imposing sanctions under MCR 2.312.

A party must file a notice of appeal within 21 days after entry of the judgment or order appealed from. If a timely postjudgment motion is filed, the notice of appeal must be filed within 21 days after entry of the order disposing of the last such pending motion. The clerk shall serve a copy of the notice on all other parties.

The trial court shall issue findings of fact and conclusions of law within 28 days after the filing of post-trial motions, or if no such motions are filed, within 28 days after the jury returns a verdict or the court makes a bench determination. The time for filing a notice of appeal runs from the entry of these findings and conclusions.

On motion of any party, the court may order that discovery be conducted in such manner as is just. The court shall specify the time, place, and scope of discovery. Orders under this rule are binding on all parties unless modified by subsequent court order. Failure to comply with a discovery order may result in sanctions prescribed by law or rule.

On motion of any party, the court may order that discovery be conducted in such sequence or manner as is just, including limiting the number of depositions or interrogatories, shortening prescribed periods, or requiring a party to proceed with discovery before another. The court shall make such orders as are necessary to prevent undue delay or expense.

On motion of a party, the court shall order discovery to proceed in stages or limit its scope if the court finds that the requested discovery is unduly burdensome, expensive, or duplicative. The court may impose conditions on the timing and manner of discovery to ensure fairness and efficiency.

A party seeking to appeal from an order granting or denying a motion for new trial must file a notice of appeal within 21 days after entry of the order. If no motion for new trial is filed, the time for filing a notice of appeal runs from the entry of judgment. The court may extend the time for good cause shown.

The court shall issue an order within 14 days after receiving the report of the attorney discipline board. If the court does not issue an order within that time, the respondent may move for a hearing on the record before the court. The motion must be filed within 28 days after the expiration of the period for issuing an order.

A party seeking review of an order from a circuit court must file a notice of appeal within 21 days after entry of the order. The notice shall be filed with the clerk of the trial court and served on all parties. Failure to file timely notice constitutes a waiver of the right to appellate review, unless excused by the court for good cause shown.

The court shall transmit the record to the appellate court within 14 days after the filing of the notice of appeal, unless a different time is specified by order. If the trial court fails to transmit the record within this period, the clerk of the appellate court may issue a writ of mandamus compelling transmission.

The court shall issue an order resolving the motion within 28 days after the filing of the response or after the time for filing a response has expired, whichever is earlier. If the court fails to issue an order within that period, the motion is deemed denied without prejudice to renewal.

A party seeking review of a final judgment or order must file a notice of appeal with the trial court clerk within 21 days after entry of the judgment or order. Failure to file a timely notice of appeal constitutes a waiver of the right to appellate review, unless good cause is shown for the delay.

A party seeking review of an order or judgment must file a notice of appeal with the trial court clerk within 21 days after entry of the order or judgment from which the appeal is taken, unless a different time is prescribed by law. Failure to file within this period constitutes a waiver of the right to appeal.

On motion of any party, the court may order that discovery be conducted in stages or that specific matters be reserved for later discovery. The court shall specify the scope and timing of such discovery. A party seeking to compel discovery beyond the ordered limits must show good cause. Failure to comply with a protective order may result in sanctions as provided by law.

The court shall enter an order resolving the motion within 28 days after filing. If the court fails to act within that period, the moving party may file a notice of expiration. Upon such filing, the court shall resolve the motion within 14 days or the motion is deemed denied without prejudice.

A party seeking to file a document under seal shall file a motion demonstrating good cause. The motion must identify the information sought to be sealed and explain why public disclosure would cause substantial harm. Unless the court orders otherwise, the moving party shall serve the motion on all parties within 7 days after filing.

The court shall enter an order granting or denying relief within 14 days after receiving the record. If the court grants relief, it shall specify the terms of the remedy. If the court denies relief, it shall state its reasons. The time for filing a notice of appeal runs from the entry of this order unless otherwise provided by law.

A party seeking to appeal an order must file a notice of appeal within 21 days after entry of the order. If a motion listed in MCR 7.205(A) is pending, the time for filing runs from entry of the order disposing of the last such motion. The clerk shall transmit the record on appeal promptly upon receipt of the required fees and proof of service.

A party seeking to appeal from a judgment or order must file a notice of appeal with the trial court within 21 days after entry of the judgment or order. If a timely motion is filed under MCR 2.612, 7.205, or 7.210, the time for filing runs from entry of the order disposing of the last such pending motion.

A party seeking review of an administrative agency decision shall file a notice of appeal with the circuit court within 42 days after the date the agency’s final order is served or mailed, whichever is earlier. Failure to file within this period deprives the court of jurisdiction unless good cause is shown for the delay.

A party seeking to file a notice of appeal shall serve a copy on all other parties within 21 days after entry of the judgment or order appealed from. The clerk of court shall transmit the record to the appellate court within 30 days after receiving the notice of appeal, unless the time is extended by agreement of the parties or order of the trial court.

A party seeking to file a notice of appeal from an order granting or denying a motion for a new trial must file the notice within 21 days after entry of the order disposing of the last timely filed motion for a new trial, unless the court extends the time on motion and for good cause shown.

A party seeking to appeal from a judgment or order must file a notice of appeal with the trial court clerk within 21 days after entry of the judgment or order sought to be reviewed. Failure to file a timely notice of appeal deprives the appellate court of jurisdiction, unless good cause is shown for the delay.

A party seeking to file an amended pleading must serve it on all other parties within 14 days after service of the original pleading. The court may, on motion or sua sponte, extend this time for good cause shown. Failure to comply with this requirement constitutes a waiver of the right to amend unless the court grants leave under MCR 2.118(C).
